Vulnerable description: The vulnerability is insufficient policy enforcement in the Resource Timing API that allows exposure of cross origin resource names, enabling browsing history inference. The root cause is a construction time state bug where the iframe state flag did_load_non_empty_document_ is initialized as false in the HTMLIFrameElement after the base frame setup runs, so early policy checks may read this flag in an incorrect state and treat the context as permissive. An attacker can craft a page that creates or navigates an iframe to cross origin targets and then reads Performance entries to observe unredacted timing names. Because the base constructor and early navigation logic execute before the member is initialized, the data and control flow let timing entries be created without proper cross origin redaction, leaking URLs and revealing a victim鈥檚 history.

The code contains a heap based buffer overflow in the HTTP chunked data path due to incomplete validation of the parsed chunk size. After reading the chunk header with strtol, the code only checks "if (c->chunk_size == 0)" and accepts any nonzero value, including negative or otherwise invalid sizes controlled by the client. An attacker can send a crafted chunked header that yields a negative chunk size, which bypasses the zero check and is then used in FFMIN to compute the recv length, causing the negative value to be converted to a very large size and leading recv to write past the end of the heap buffer. This flawed data and control flow from unvalidated parsing to buffer write enables memory corruption. Exploiting this overflow can allow remote code execution in affected FFmpeg ffserver versions.

The function FinishCurrentUtterance is vulnerable to reentrancy induced use after free because the non null check on current_utterance_ gates a call to FinishAndDestroy while the pointer is only cleared afterward. If FinishAndDestroy triggers callbacks that re enter the controller, the function can run again before nulling occurs, allowing the same object to pass the guard and be destroyed twice. The control and data flow thus loop from the guard to the destructive call and back to the guard while the state update lags, exposing a dangling pointer window. An attacker who can influence these callbacks or timing can cause denial of service through crashes and may escalate to memory corruption with potential for code execution.

The code is vulnerable to a predictable hash collision attack that allows hashtable operations to degrade to linear time and consume excessive CPU. The root cause is deterministic bucket selection without randomization or collision mitigation, as the index is computed by first deriving a predictable hash with hash = hash_str(key) and then indexing with bucket = &hashtable->buckets[hash % num_buckets(hashtable)]. An attacker can supply many distinct keys that collide to the same hash value so they all map to one bucket, causing hashtable_find_pair to traverse an increasingly long chain on every access. This enables denial of service by driving CPU usage to extreme levels, matching the behavior described in the referenced Jansson CVE.

The FITS image loader contains an input validation flaw that allows attacker controlled header fields to drive unsafe size calculations and memory use. The root cause is that values parsed from the header via StringToLong are stored in int members such as columns and rows without bounds or sign checks, then used to compute the pixel count in an unsigned size type, so negative or extreme values become very large. An attacker can craft a FITS header with naxis1 or naxis2 set to extreme or negative numbers, causing the computed number of pixels to be enormous while the code only checks that it is not zero, which leads downstream allocation or read loops to overrun buffers or crash the process. Data flows from ReadBlob into value, through StringToLong into fits_info fields, and directly into the pixel count and subsequent image processing logic, enabling the exploit path. Additionally, repeated COMMENT cards are concatenated without a size limit using ConcatenateString, enabling memory exhaustion and denial of service.

The code is vulnerable due to type confusion and insufficient validation of MAPI attributes parsed from untrusted TNEF MAPIPROPS data. In the message branch, entries returned by mapi_attr_read are trusted and the code immediately dereferences fields such as a->name in the comparison if a->name == MAPI_BODY_HTML and then uses other fields like a->num_values to size and process body buffers. An attacker can craft a MAPIPROPS blob that causes mapi_attr_read to yield mis typed or malformed MAPI_Attr structures so that the dereference of a->name and subsequent processing operate on invalid or attacker controlled data. This data flow from attr->buf into mapi_attrs and then into the branch for HTML body handling leads to invalid reads and writes in memory. The result can be a crash, information disclosure, heap corruption, and potentially arbitrary code execution.

The jpc_bitstream_getbits function in JasPer before 2.0.10 contains an assertion based denial of service. The root cause is reliance on an assert as the only check that the caller supplied n is within 0 to 31, rather than performing robust runtime validation. An attacker can feed a crafted image that causes the decoder to pass a very large integer to this function, which triggers the assert and terminates the process. The parameter flows directly from the function entry into the assert with no prior sanitization, so failing the predicate immediately aborts execution and enables a remote crash during image parsing.

The vulnerability is a buffer over read in tcpdump鈥檚 ISO IS-IS parser function isis_print_id that processes System IDs. It occurs because the loop iterates with for i equals 1 to SYSTEM_ID_LEN and dereferences cp via *cp++ without validating that id_len provides at least that many bytes, so the loop bound is fixed while the available input length is not. An attacker can trigger this by supplying an IS-IS packet with a System ID shorter than SYSTEM_ID_LEN, causing the function to read past the end of the provided buffer. The data and control flow use a constant iteration count independent of id_len and snprintf only constrains the destination buffer, leading to an out of bounds read that can crash tcpdump or potentially disclose adjacent memory.

The provided function exsltDateCreateDate is not the source of the vulnerability, as it allocates with xmlMalloc, checks for null, and zero initializes the structure before setting fields, which is safe. The actual flaw in the affected libxslt versions lies in numbers.c where namespace nodes are mishandled, causing out of bounds heap memory access during number formatting. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted XSLT document that drives the numbers handling logic to traverse or index namespace nodes without proper bounds checks. The data and control flow within numbers processing fails to validate indices and node counts, which leads to memory being accessed past allocated regions and can result in denial of service or potentially other unintended impact.

The function contains a memory management vulnerability caused by mismatched allocation and deallocation of the buffer referenced by "OBJECT_NAME_INFORMATION* name". After probing NtQueryObject for the required size, the code allocates an array with "new BYTE[size]" and then hands ownership to scoped_ptr<OBJECT_NAME_INFORMATION>, which will later release it with scalar delete instead of delete[], leading to undefined behavior and possible heap corruption. This flaw is triggered whenever GetPathFromHandle is invoked and the NtQueryObject call returns a size that causes the array allocation and subsequent smart pointer reset. The data and control flow from resolving and calling NtQueryObject through allocating the buffer and relying on scoped_ptr to free it directly produces the delete versus delete[] mismatch. An attacker who can influence execution paths or heap state may exploit the resulting corruption to crash the process or potentially achieve code execution.

The code in SplashOutputDev::drawSoftMaskedImage contains an integer overflow that leads to a heap buffer overflow when allocating the color lookup table for RGB8 or BGR8 images. The root cause is that n is computed as a left shift of one by the bit depth from untrusted image metadata without bounds checking and then used to allocate a buffer sized at three times n while arithmetic is performed in a narrow integer type. An attacker can craft a PDF that sets a large bit depth with a single component color map so control reaches the RGB path, causing the allocation to be undersized while the subsequent loop writes three bytes per iteration for i from zero to n. This mismatch between the overflowed allocation size and the unbounded write loop can corrupt heap memory, resulting in denial of service or potentially remote code execution.

The code exposes a GCM mode IV reuse flaw in the Ruby openssl gem when the IV is set before the key, undermining both confidentiality and integrity. In ossl_cipher_set_key the function enforces key length and then calls EVP_CipherInit_ex with the IV argument set to NULL and enc set to minus one, which preserves any previously configured IV instead of reinitializing it for the newly applied key. As a result, if a caller first sets the IV and then sets the key, the same IV can be reused with that key across encryption operations. An attacker who observes ciphertexts produced with the same key and IV in GCM can exploit nonce reuse to recover plaintext and forge authentication tags.

A buffer overflow exists in the ImageMagick SUN image decoder before 6.9.0-4 Beta that can be triggered by a crafted SUN file, resulting in a crash. The root cause is insufficient bounds and consistency validation of header controlled sizes such as "maplength" and "length" together with width, height, and depth, which are used to size colormap and pixel buffers but are later overrun during palette loading or pixel decoding. An attacker can supply a SUN header with valid magic and allowed types yet with a malicious "maptype" and an oversized or inconsistent "maplength" so that image->colors and related line sizes are computed from attacker input, allocations are made via AcquireImageColormap or AcquireQuantumMemory, and subsequent writes exceed those allocations. The data flow reads the untrusted fields with ReadBlobMSBLong, derives image->colors from "maplength" or "maplength" divided by 3, computes per line or pixel counts, and then performs palette reads and unpacking that write past the end of the allocated buffers. Successful exploitation causes memory corruption and a denial of service and could enable further unintended behavior depending on the environment.

The code handling drag and drop in OnPerformDrop is vulnerable because it accepts any syntactically valid URL from untrusted drop data and forwards it to the tab strip. The root cause is the conditional that only checks GetURLAndTitle and url.is_valid and then unconditionally calls mapped_data.SetURL and forwards the event, without enforcing a safe scheme or navigation policy. An attacker can trigger this by dropping a URL that is valid yet dangerous such as javascript, data, file, or chrome so it passes the check and is propagated to the navigation handler. The data flow shows event.data feeding the URL at the vulnerable check, guarded only by forwarding_to_tab_strip, after which the mapped event is forwarded to tabstrip navigation. This can lead to unintended or privileged navigations and potential script execution or information disclosure via unsafe schemes.

Chrome contained a use after free in its PDF processing component that allowed a crafted document to trigger access to freed objects. The root cause was improper lifetime management in which PDF objects were freed during teardown while asynchronous callbacks or event handlers still retained references, leaving dangling pointers. By crafting a PDF that provokes specific parsing states and forces component cleanup while tasks or notifications remain queued, the control flow later invokes handlers that operate on already freed memory. This flaw can be exploited to crash the process for denial of service and may enable further impact such as arbitrary code execution.

This code is vulnerable to a use after free arising from destructor re entry in the Networking Disk Cache. In OnEntryDestroyEnd the call to "DecreaseNumRefs" can drop the last reference and trigger object destruction or invalidate "data_", yet the function immediately evaluates "data_->header.num_bytes" without ensuring the object is still alive, which constitutes a lifetime and reentrancy bug. An attacker can trigger this by causing a crafted sequence of cache entry creations and destructions via web content so that the reference count reaches zero during destruction, after which the conditional is evaluated and accesses freed memory. The flaw occurs during condition evaluation and can corrupt memory, enabling remote code execution as described for Chrome prior to 66.0.3359.117.

ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 contains a buffer overflow in the exception handling subsystem where accumulating too many exceptions overflows an internal storage buffer, causing a crash. The root cause is the absence of a strict bound on the number of stored exceptions, so each new exception is appended without limit, eventually writing past the allocated memory. A crafted VIFF file can trigger this by provoking repeated failures during parsing, for example by using an invalid identifier or inconsistent dimensions that lead to EOFBlob while the code continues reading header fields with functions like ReadBlobLong and then calling ThrowReaderException. As the decoder loop processes untrusted header data, each error condition generates another exception that is pushed into the unbounded buffer in memory.c, resulting in an overflow and a reliable denial of service.

This code contains a use after free in the Blink AttributeSetter path that handles document.location. The root cause is taking a raw pointer via "TestNode* imp = WTF::getPtr(proxyImp->locationWithException())", which drops lifetime protection and leaves imp vulnerable to becoming dangling when subsequent operations convert jsValue or otherwise run script and reenter the engine. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted document.location value whose stringification or side effects execute during attribute setting, freeing or detaching the underlying object while imp remains cached. The data and control flow from info.Holder to V8TestObject::toNative to locationWithException to WTF::getPtr yields imp, after which the code invokes "imp->setHrefThrows" on a potentially freed object, enabling remote denial of service and possibly other impact.

The vulnerability is an initialization order flaw in the paint property tree setup where the effect root is obtained early via "current_effect(EffectPaintPropertyNode::Root())" before the clip, transform, and scroll roots are established. This occurs because the effect root is fetched in the constructor initializer while the other roots are assigned in the constructor body, which can yield an inconsistent or stale effect node if the underlying root is not yet initialized or synchronized. An attacker can trigger the flaw by supplying content that exercises complex combinations of effects with absolute or fixed positioning, causing the renderer to traverse mismatched property trees and dereference invalid state. The resulting inconsistency can crash the browser leading to denial of service and may enable other undefined behavior.

The code is vulnerable because the SSLv2 server handshake fails to enforce the configured cipher policy, allowing disabled ciphers to remain usable. During ClientHello processing, the server builds a client derived list and attempts to intersect it with the server allowed list using the loop that calls "sk_SSL_CIPHER_find(allow, sk_SSL_CIPHER_value(prio, z))", but the result of this filtering is never committed because the intended assignment of the filtered list back to the session is effectively disabled. An attacker can trigger this by sending an SSLv2 ClientHello that advertises weak or disabled ciphers, which the server erroneously preserves and later negotiates since the intersection logic does not take effect. As a result, disabled ciphers can be selected, enabling man in the middle attacks that exploit weak SSLv2 cryptography and undermining the intended cryptographic protections.

The function ptrace_setxregs is vulnerable to kernel information disclosure because it copies data from a user supplied pointer without validating the address space. It casts the user pointer to a non user annotated type and then uses "__copy_from_user" on addresses derived from that pointer, for example "&xtregs->cp0" and "&xtregs->opt", without an access_ok check, which allows reads from arbitrary kernel addresses. An attacker can trigger this by issuing a crafted PTRACE_SETXTREGS request that supplies kernel space addresses instead of user space buffers. The copied data is stored in kernel structures such as ti->xtregs_cp and regs->xtregs_opt and can later be exposed back to user space through corresponding get paths, enabling leakage of sensitive kernel memory.

The code is vulnerable to improper access control because the untrusted parameter call_name directly selects which RPC or method is executed without validation. The root cause is that call_name is fed into StringToIdentifier and the resulting id is passed through InitParams and into plugin->Invoke with no whitelist or authorization check tying the name to an allowed set for the given call type or caller. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted call_name that maps to internal or privileged operations which the code will initialize and invoke as long as the supplied arguments match the expected signature. This data and control flow allows unauthorized method dispatch and can lead to state manipulation, information disclosure, or other unintended side effects depending on the capabilities exposed by the targeted method.

The vulnerability is an improper input validation flaw in the WARC parser function _warc_read that allows a tiny crafted file to cause near infinite runtime and excessive disk usage. It occurs because the code treats a premature lack of input as a clean end of record by jumping to eof when __archive_read_ahead returns zero and then setting *off = w->cntoff + 4U and returning ARCHIVE_EOF even when w->cntoff is still less than the declared content length. An attacker can trigger this by advertising a large Content Length in a WARC record while providing little or no body data so the read loop repeatedly believes it has reached a valid end and advances past a non existent trailer without ever validating that the promised bytes were actually read. This faulty control flow causes the archive read machinery to spin or repeatedly manage buffers and temporary storage leading to a denial of service through extreme CPU time and disk consumption.

The function unregisterBlobURL contains a thread safety vulnerability where shared state is modified before thread affinity is enforced. When the origin of the URL equals null, the code removes the entry from the origin map on the calling thread, then only afterward checks isMainThread to decide whether to marshal the remaining unregister to the main thread. This sequencing lets calls from worker threads update the origin map concurrently with main thread operations, creating a data race that can corrupt registry state or crash the process. An attacker who can trigger blob URL unregistration from a worker context can exploit this race to cause denial of service and potentially other unspecified impact.

The clie_5_attach function in drivers/usb/serial/visor.c has a null pointer dereference vulnerability due to inadequate validation of required USB bulk out resources. The only guard is "if (serial->num_ports < 2) return -1;" which allows execution to proceed assuming that serial->port[1] exposes a valid bulk out endpoint and that write URBs are allocated. When a USB device lacking a bulk out endpoint is inserted, the code copies serial->port[1]->bulk_out_endpointAddress, builds a bulk pipe, and then assigns to port->write_urbs[j]->pipe, which can be NULL and causes a system crash. A physically proximate attacker can trigger this with a crafted USB device, leading to denial of service and potentially other unspecified impact.

The function regulator_ena_gpio_free in the Linux kernel contains a use after free bug that can allow a local user to gain privileges or cause a denial of service. The root cause is that when a list entry matches the device enable pin, the code releases the GPIO and removes the list node via gpiod_put, list_del, and kfree but leaves rdev->ena_pin pointing to the freed object and does not stop iterating. The bug is triggered when the loop finds a match using the comparison "pin->gpiod == rdev->ena_pin->gpiod" while the request counter is at or below one, after which subsequent evaluations of rdev->ena_pin->gpiod in the loop or later paths dereference freed memory. This data and control flow results in immediate or subsequent use after free, enabling crafted interactions with the regulator subsystem to crash the kernel or potentially execute code with elevated privileges.

The code is vulnerable to unsafe cache pathname construction that enables path traversal in NeoMutt before 2018-07-16. The function builds a cache filename by calling snprintf with the format "%s.hcache" and passes the untrusted path directly, with no sanitization of slash characters or traversal sequences. An attacker can supply a path containing slashes or sequences such as ../ to influence the resulting cache path when the header cache is created or accessed. Because the path parameter flows unmodified into the filesystem name, the attacker can redirect cache files outside the intended directory, potentially creating or overwriting arbitrary files, poisoning cache entries, or causing denial of service.

The function isis_print_mt_capability_subtlv contains a buffer over-read in the ISO IS-IS parser of tcpdump. The root cause is the lack of a bounds check before reading the first two bytes of each subTLV with the statements "stlv_type = *(tptr++)" and "stlv_len = *(tptr++)", while the loop is gated only by a logical length variable rather than the actual captured buffer size. An attacker can trigger this by crafting a truncated IS-IS packet so that fewer than two bytes remain at the current pointer while len is still greater than two, leading to an out-of-bounds read before any ND_TCHECK2 safeguards are applied. The control flow enters the loop on len, immediately performs the unguarded reads, and only afterward applies checks, allowing tptr to advance past the available data. Successful exploitation can crash the parser and may expose adjacent memory, resulting in denial of service or information disclosure.

The code exhibits a use after free in the IndexedDB path where thread affinity is enforced only by the debug鈥憃nly assertion "DCHECK(idb_thread_checker_.CalledOnValidThread())". The root cause is reliance on a nonproduction check with no runtime synchronization or lifetime guarantees, so in release builds a call can arrive on the wrong thread and still proceed if IsConnected returns true. An attacker can trigger this by crafting HTML that drives racy IndexedDB operations so that "CreateTransaction" executes after the underlying connection or database object has been freed on another thread. Because the control flow unconditionally calls connection_->database()->CreateTransaction when connected, stale pointers can be dereferenced, enabling out of bounds memory reads and a potential sandbox escape.

The function common_timer_get contains an integer overflow in overrun accounting at the statement "timr->it_overrun += (int)kc->timer_forward(timr, now)". The root cause is a narrowing cast to int and an int based accumulator while kc->timer_forward may return a large expiration count that exceeds INT_MAX. An attacker can create a periodic POSIX timer with a very small interval and delay servicing via timer_create and timer_settime so that many expirations accumulate and the update path is executed. Because kc is obtained from timr->kclock and the returned count flows directly into the int addition without bounds checks, the value wraps and corrupts it_overrun, producing user visible random results via timer_getoverrun and siginfo.si_overrun and enabling denial of service through signed integer overflow.

The aesdecode implementation is vulnerable to uninitialized memory use that can crash the interpreter or enable code execution. The root cause is that after allocating the AES context the code validates the key length and emits a rangecheck error but does not abort, then unconditionally invokes "aes_setkey_dec" with state controlled key bytes and bit length, so an absent or malformed key leaves the key material uninitialized. An attacker can trigger this by supplying crafted PostScript that sets aesdecode parameters to an invalid key length or omits the key so the code path that throws "invalid aes key length" still proceeds to key schedule setup. The data and control flow take attacker controlled state keylength and state key through the unchecked call to "aes_setkey_dec" which reads from uninitialized memory and uses it in decryption, leading to crashes and potentially arbitrary code execution.

The function Segment::GetFirst is vulnerable because it can return an invalid pointer when it accesses "m_clusters[0]" after only verifying that the array pointer is non null and the count is positive. The root cause is reliance on a debug assert to validate "pCluster" instead of a runtime check, so in release builds a null or corrupted first entry produced by parsing untrusted media is returned to callers. An attacker can craft a WebM or related media file that drives mkvparser to create a non empty m_clusters array whose first element is null or otherwise invalid, which passes the guard and is then propagated without validation. Downstream code in mediaserver and libvpx that dereferences the returned pointer can crash or corrupt memory, enabling denial of service and potentially remote code execution as described in the Android advisory for bug 23452792.

The vulnerability is an authorization flaw in libvirt where virDomainGetTime can be invoked over a read only connection even though a read write connection is required. It occurs because the wrapper performs only a domain validity check and then directly dispatches to the driver callback without enforcing connection permissions, as it executes the driver method when available and returns the result with no access control gate. An attacker with a read only handle can trigger it by calling virDomainGetTime, which the code forwards to the guest agent through dom->conn->driver->domainGetTime regardless of connection mode. This control flow bypass allows unauthorized use of guest agent functionality via an RO connection, enabling a privilege bypass and unintended information disclosure about guest time and timing state that should be restricted to RW clients.

The code is vulnerable to a denial of service due to using an incompletely read event structure to drive control flow. After reading from the UHID device with "ret = read(p_dev->fd, &ev, sizeof(ev))", the code immediately tests "ev.type" and switches on it without first ensuring that at least the event type field was read, so a short read leaves "ev.type" uninitialized or defaulted from the prior memset. A crafted application can send a signal to the Bluetooth process that interrupts the read and causes such partial reads, leading the handler to misclassify the event and perform incorrect state transitions or enter code paths that assume valid data. This tainted control decision can destabilize the Bluetooth stack and crash or hang the service, resulting in loss of Bluetooth functionality including emergency use cases.

The code contains a buffer overflow in the Base64 decoding path. The root cause is that a fixed size destination "char buffer[16]" is passed to "mutt_b64_decode(buffer, encoded)" without conveying the buffer capacity or enforcing bounds, so the decoder may write past the end of the array. An attacker can trigger this by supplying base64 input that decodes to more than 16 bytes, and the subsequent write "buffer[len] = '\0'" can also go out of bounds if the returned length is too large or negative. The data flow allocates a small buffer, passes it unchecked to the decoder, then trusts the returned length, which can lead to memory corruption, process crashes, or potential code execution.

The vulnerability is a NULL pointer dereference in the NFSv4 open release path that can be exploited to crash the kernel. It occurs because the code only checks whether the state pointer is an error value and fails to verify that it is non NULL before calling nfs4_close_state, allowing a NULL state to be used. A local user can trigger this via mknod on an NFSv4 filesystem which exercises encode_share_access in a way that results in an invalid or missing open state so that nfs4_opendata_to_nfs4_state returns NULL. Due to the incomplete guard, control flows to the call site with a NULL state and the subsequent dereference triggers a kernel BUG leading to a denial of service.

The function next_format contains a vulnerability where the pointer parameter palette_number is dereferenced and modified without validation, for example in "++*palette_number" and "*palette_number = 0". The root cause is the unconditional trust in caller supplied pointers, as control and data flow from colour_type and bit_depth lead to multiple paths that write through palette_number with no null or bounds checks. An attacker can trigger this by providing crafted image data that steers the decoder into paths such as the bit depth equals zero case or the colour type equals three case, causing a write through an invalid palette pointer. The resulting invalid memory access can crash a privileged component and in affected Android versions this was part of an unspecified libpng flaw that could be leveraged by a crafted application to gain elevated privileges.

The vulnerability is an ASLR bypass in arch_pick_mmap_layout where the legacy mmap base is not properly randomized on x86 kernels through 4.5.2. The root cause is that the code computes the legacy base as "mm->mmap_legacy_base = mmap_legacy_base(random_factor)" with random_factor often remaining zero, and the legacy path fails to enforce sufficient entropy for privileged executions. A local user can trigger the legacy layout by disabling stack consumption limits, for example by setting an unlimited stack, causing the function to use a predictable base. The data flow from the zero initialization of random_factor into mmap_legacy_base and then into the selected legacy mmap base yields a deterministic address even when ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE should be ineffective for setuid or setgid programs. As a result, an attacker can bypass ASLR for setuid or setgid binaries and significantly ease exploitation through predictable memory mappings.

GPAC 0.7.1 contains a memory leak in dinf_Read where a default data reference box is allocated when the parsed dinf lacks a dref. The root cause is that after gf_isom_box_array_read parses child boxes, the code detects the missing dref, logs "Missing dref box in dinf," then creates a new box with gf_isom_box_new and returns success without integrating the object into the managed box array or arranging its deallocation. An attacker can trigger this by providing an input bitstream that omits the dref, which steers control flow into the allocation path and leaves the newly created object outside the normal ownership and cleanup lifecycle. Repeatedly opening such crafted files can accumulate unreleased allocations and lead to memory exhaustion and denial of service.

The vulnerability is an information disclosure in ABRT event scripts that copy sosreport files into problem directories with world readable permissions. The root cause is that the scripts create or copy the sosreport without enforcing a restrictive mode or umask and do not subsequently correct the file permissions, leaving the copy accessible to all local users. It is triggered whenever ABRT handles a crash and generates or archives a sosreport in a problem directory, where the resulting file includes sensitive data such as content from var log messages. As the control flow writes the sosreport to a shared location without restricting access to the owner, any unprivileged local user can read the file and extract system information, configuration details, and potentially secrets from system logs.

This code is vulnerable to command injection in ss-manager due to constructing a shell command from untrusted configuration fields without proper validation or escaping. The root cause is that untrusted data from the JSON manager request is assigned at "char *method = manager->method" and later inserted unquoted into the command string via snprintf such as "%s -m %s", with similar exposure for other fields like manager address, nameservers, and hosts. An attacker can trigger the flaw by sending a crafted JSON request over localhost UDP with shell metacharacters in method or related fields, which flow through add_server and build_config into construct_command_line and produce a malicious command that is executed by a shell. This enables execution of arbitrary commands with the privileges of the ss-manager process.

The code is vulnerable because it passes an untrusted mode parameter directly into the decoder configuration without validation. The root cause is the unchecked use of a value retrieved by GET_PARAM to select the decoding mode, which can be influenced by attacker controlled media metadata. A crafted media file can supply an out of range or unexpected mode so that SetMode configures the codec into an invalid state. The control and data flow shows that after initialization the mode value flows directly from GET_PARAM to SetMode with no sanitization, allowing this misconfiguration to reach libvpx decoding paths and violate memory access assumptions. This can lead to memory corruption, denial of service, or remote code execution as observed in Android mediaserver processing of malformed WebM or MKV inputs.

The code contains a stack based buffer overflow in receive_tcppacket where untrusted input length is copied into a fixed size stack buffer without bounds checking. The root cause is that the function sets outpkt.len to the caller supplied len and then copies len bytes from buffer into outpkt.data with no validation against the capacity of outpkt.data and with an unsafe implicit conversion from signed int to size_t. A remote authenticated peer can trigger this by sending an oversized TCP packet so that len exceeds the destination buffer size. Because len and buffer flow directly from the caller to the copy operation with no guards, the stack allocated structure is overrun, enabling denial of service through a crash and potentially arbitrary code execution.

The code is vulnerable to heap buffer overflow in bitmap scaling due to a bad cast and unchecked arithmetic in the row stride calculation. The root cause is that rowBytes is computed as a size_t cast of resizeWidth multiplied by the number of bytes per pixel without overflow validation, which can wrap for large values and yield a stride smaller than width times bytes per pixel. An attacker can supply crafted HTML or image content that drives resizeWidth and resizeHeight to extreme values, causing the scaling routine to write resizeHeight rows using the undersized stride into the destination buffer. The data flow passes attacker influenced dimensions directly into the stride calculation and then into SkPixmap, after which the scaling code copies more data than the buffer can hold, corrupting heap memory. This enables denial of service or potential remote code execution.

The function config_save contains a heap buffer overflow stemming from incorrect allocation sizing. The root cause is an unchecked integer overflow in the expression "osi_calloc(strlen(filename) + 5)" which can wrap for extremely long attacker controlled filenames, after which the code performs "strcpy(temp_filename, filename)" and "strcat(temp_filename, .new)" into a too small buffer. This can be triggered by a crafted application that influences the Bluetooth process to invoke this routine with an excessively long filename, as the code only asserts non NULL and non empty and directly feeds the value into strlen for allocation. The data flows from the external filename to the size calculation to allocation and then to the copy and append operations, causing memory corruption and a crash of the Bluetooth process that leads to denial of service and loss of Bluetooth 911 functionality.

The ip_gre module in affected Linux kernels has a race condition during initialization that exposes the GRE receive handler before required state is prepared. The root cause is registering the protocol first through the call to inet_add_protocol which makes the handler reachable while per net structures and link operations have not been initialized. An attacker can trigger this by sending a GRE packet during module load, causing the handler to run against uninitialized or null state. This premature exposure and control flow window leads to invalid memory access and a kernel oops, enabling a remote denial of service.

The function contains an out of bounds heap write due to a flawed loop condition in the per plane processing, written as "in->data[plane] && plane < 4". Because the left operand is evaluated first, a crafted frame that makes an extra plane pointer non NULL can cause the loop to run with plane values beyond the intended 0 to 3 range. The loop then indexes fixed size arrays such as w[4] and h[4] and passes these along with out->data[plane] into hblur and vblur, which perform writes using an invalid plane index, corrupting heap memory. An attacker who provides a crafted input frame can trigger this condition remotely, leading to a crash or arbitrary memory corruption and potentially code execution.

The code is vulnerable because it populates reference picture maps using counts and lists derived directly from the bitstream and a potentially inconsistent decoded picture buffer, then dereferences entries and writes mapping pointers without validating existence or capacity. In ih264d_parse_bslice the loops are bounded by the bitstream supplied values in u1_num_ref_idx_lx_active and they index ps_dec->ps_ref_pic_buf_lx and dereference ps_pic->pu1_buf1 with no null checks, while the MBAFF paths write two entries per reference into ppv_map_ref_idx_to_poc without demonstrating sufficient bounds. An attacker can trigger the flaw with a crafted H.264 stream that manipulates MMCO and reference list reordering so that the DPB contains fewer or invalid entries than requested, after which the function trusts these lists and counts and performs invalid reads and writes. This data flow from untrusted bitstream fields through unchecked DPB state to pointer dereferences and array writes can cause memory corruption and denial of service, and under the conditions described by the cited CVE may enable remote code execution.

The vulnerability is a lack of bounds checking when deriving and serializing a cached resource type to JSON, which can lead to out of bounds access and heap corruption. The root cause is that the function forwards the incoming cached resource directly into helper routines that compute a type and serialize it without validating the range or integrity of the resulting values. An attacker can trigger this by crafting HTML that drives WebRTC to supply a resource with malformed or out of range metadata, causing the downstream routines to index tables or write into buffers beyond valid limits. Because the only statement consumes the parameter and immediately invokes the helpers with no guards, the invalid state propagates unchecked, enabling heap corruption and potentially remote code execution or a browser crash.

The function decoder_peek_si_internal contains a buffer over read when decryption is enabled because it decrypts at most nine bytes into a fixed stack buffer defined as "uint8_t clear_buffer[9]" and then parses the bitstream from this small buffer. The root cause is the mismatch between the limited decrypted buffer and the amount of header data the bitreader consumes before adequate size validation, allowing reads past the end of clear_buffer. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted media file that forces the decrypt path and causes the parser to read more than nine bytes of header fields. The control flow sets data to the small buffer after decrypt_cb is called and initializes the bit reader on it, then performs multiple vpx_rb_read operations before later size checks, leading to an out of bounds read on the stack. In Android mediaserver this results in denial of service such as a crash, hang, or reboot.

This code is vulnerable to SQL injection in msPostGISLayerSetTimeFilter when handling WMS Time input. The root cause is construction of SQL filter text by concatenating untrusted timestring tokens into a buffer without strict validation or escaping, which bounded string functions do not prevent. An attacker can supply a crafted WMS Time value that injects SQL fragments, which are split into tokens, turned into comparison snippets by the helper builders, appended into the final filter buffer, and then loaded into lp->filter for inclusion in the PostGIS query. Successful exploitation allows remote execution of arbitrary SQL on the backend, enabling data exfiltration or modification and potential service disruption.

The ff_mpeg4_decode_picture_header function in FFmpeg 4.0 contains a denial of service vulnerability where an inconsistent bits per sample value can trigger an assertion during decoding. The root cause is insufficient validation in the studio profile path, which only checks that bits per raw sample is nonzero and then proceeds to decode_studio_vop_header, failing to ensure the value is within a valid range and consistent with the parsed headers. An attacker can craft an AVI that sets the studio profile through profile level parsing and embeds a contradictory bits per raw sample value in header data, which passes the minimal check and reaches code that asserts on invariant violations. The control flow parses start codes, enables studio profile, performs only a presence check on bits per raw sample, and then invokes downstream decoding where the assertion fires, causing a crash and resulting in denial of service.

The function contains a memory leak caused by allocating a SettingInfo with raw new and never releasing it. Specifically, the code allocates with "auto* info = new content_settings::SettingInfo();" then passes the pointer to GetWebsiteSetting and later reads info->source when constructing results, but no path frees or transfers ownership of info. Any invocation that reaches this allocation leaks memory, including paths that return early after failed parsing of the stored object list as well as the normal success path. An attacker who can cause repeated calls to this code can drive unbounded heap growth and potentially achieve denial of service.

AsyncPixelTransfersCompletedQuery::End contains an out of bounds shared memory access vulnerability. The root cause is that it only verifies that buffer.shared_memory is non null and does not ensure that shm_data_offset plus shm_data_size lies within buffer.size. An attacker can trigger this by causing shm_offset to produce a value such that the offset plus the size of QuerySync exceeds the shared memory segment, after which these unvalidated parameters are packed into AsyncMemoryParams and used by the asynchronous completion routine to access memory. Through this data flow from shm_offset into mem_params and then into the completion processing, the code can read or write past the end of the shared buffer, leading to GPU command buffer memory corruption, denial of service, or other impact.

The NavigateGuest logic is vulnerable to a same origin policy bypass because it relies on GetOrigin comparisons while explicitly exempting about:blank. The root cause is the condition that marks a URL as allowed when the resolved value equals about:blank which skips the same origin restriction against the extension origin. An attacker can pass a crafted src that resolves to about:blank so that src flows through Resolve to url to the url_not_allowed flag and then to the navigation call, resulting in a successful load. This allows an about:blank document to inherit the extension origin and can expose privileged extension data or enable script execution with extension privileges as captured by the Chrome Extensions CVE.

The function SpeechFinished is vulnerable to a use after free due to calling SendResponse followed by Release, where SendResponse may synchronously drop the last reference and destroy the object, leaving Release to operate on freed memory. The root cause is lifetime mismanagement of the ExtensionTtsSpeakFunction object, with no self retention or ordering that guarantees the object remains valid after SendResponse. The flaw is triggered whenever SpeechFinished runs and the control flow from function entry unconditionally reads the error, computes success, invokes SendResponse with that value, and then proceeds to Release without any guard. An attacker who can influence the timing or conditions under which SendResponse finalizes the object can cause memory corruption or a process crash and under certain conditions may escalate to arbitrary code execution.

The code is vulnerable to a denial of service stemming from Jansson鈥檚 predictable hash collisions when parsing JSON objects. The root cause is that the Jansson library up to certain versions does not randomize or sufficiently protect its object key hashing, allowing an attacker to craft many colliding keys that force worst case hash table behavior. This program reads untrusted data from the input file and feeds it directly into the parser via "json_loadf" or "json_loads" after an optional strip step, with no size limits or parsing time controls. As a result, attacker controlled JSON can drive excessive collision handling inside the parser, causing extreme CPU consumption and rendering the application unresponsive.

No vulnerability is evident in the provided constructor for MdSettingsUI, which solely initializes a WebUI controller and registers predefined handlers and static resources. There is no root cause for a flaw because the code does not accept or process untrusted input, and calls like AddSettingsPageUIHandler and WebUIDataSource::Add follow standard ownership and lifecycle patterns. The control and data flow are deterministic and driven by constants such as chrome::kChromeUIMdSettingsHost and IDR_SETTINGS_SETTINGS_HTML, with no tainted inputs reaching sensitive operations. Consequently, an attacker cannot leverage this snippet to achieve code execution, information disclosure, or privilege escalation.

The vulnerability is an out of bounds palette access in image_pixel_init when handling paletted PNG data. It occurs because the function accepts a raw palette pointer as store_palette palette with no associated size and then indexes it using a data derived this->palette_index without any bounds validation, only checking that palette is non null. An attacker can craft image data so that sample produces an index that exceeds the actual palette length, leading the code to read from palette[i] while populating red, green, blue and alpha. This data and control flow from untrusted row and colour_type into the palette branch culminates in an invalid memory read, which can crash the process or disclose memory and in the context of libpng before 1.6.20 on Android could contribute to privilege escalation as described by the CVE.

No buffer overflow is evident in the provided CUT image reader, as it validates header fields, constrains depth to fixed values, and allocates the colormap based on the palette MaxIndex before filling it. The control flow guards all blob reads and seeks, decrements the encoded size consistently, and aborts on inconsistencies, which prevents overruns during run length decoding and palette parsing. Data flow from the file to memory is bounded by checks such as rejecting zero dimensions, enforcing expected encoded byte counts, and ensuring i stays within the allocated colormap range. A crafted file would trigger error paths and be rejected, so the buffer overflow described for ReadVIFFImage in a different module does not apply to this code.

The code in fs aio iovec setup is vulnerable to an integer overflow that allows a local user to craft a very large AIO iovec and cause denial of service or possibly other impacts. The root cause is that the helper which sums user supplied iovec lengths can overflow and still return a nonnegative total, after which the function only checks if ret < 0 and then unconditionally assigns ki_nbytes and ki_left to the wrapped value. An attacker can pass a large segment count in kiocb->ki_nbytes and large lengths via kiocb->ki_buf so that rw_copy_check_uvector or its compat variant computes a truncated ret which is accepted as valid. This data flow leaves the kiocb with inconsistent sizes, causing subsequent AIO processing to operate on incorrect lengths, leading to kernel crashes or other unpredictable behavior.

The function is vulnerable because it dereferences a potentially invalid iterator obtained from cached_chunk when copying a cached subsequence, using values such as "cached_chunk->id" without a release mode validity check. The root cause is reliance on DCHECKs for iterator and state validation, which are removed in production, so if FindChunkByDisplayItemIndex returns the end iterator due to an invalid begin index or inconsistent paint chunks, the subsequent dereference proceeds unchecked. The data and control flow show that the update call drawing from cached_chunk depends on the input parameters begin_index and end_index and only a debug time assertion, allowing crafted or malformed rendering state to trigger the flaw. An attacker could cause a browser crash leading to denial of service and possibly other undefined effects, consistent with the impact reported for Chrome versions before 47.0.2526.73.

The vulnerability is an unsafe uAPI in the InfiniBand stack where complex command structures with embedded user pointers are accepted through the write path, enabling unintended kernel memory writes and denial of service. The root cause is reliance on the write system call for a pointer bearing ABI without compat translation or strict pointer validation, so pointer fields copied from userspace are interpreted using kernel native layout and size, especially across 32 bit to 64 bit boundaries. An attacker can trigger it by issuing a crafted write that sets cmd.type and supplies malicious values for fields such as user_info.spu_base_info or ctxt_info, after which qib_write copies the structure and forwards those pointers to helpers like qib_get_base_info or qib_ctxt_info that perform kernel to user writes, thereby writing to attacker controlled addresses. This data flow from user buffer to kernel struct to helper routines leads to memory corruption and system crashes, with potential for unspecified further impact.

The code dispatches onTabUpdated events that can include a tab URL to all extensions without verifying that the recipient has the tabs permission. The function takes DictionaryValue* changed_properties and WebContents* contents, appends the properties to the event arguments, and calls BroadcastEvent, but performs no permission gating such as enforcing APIPermission::kTab. When a tab updates, the URL embedded in changed_properties flows from the parameters through args_base construction directly into the broadcast, so extensions without the required permission can receive it. An attacker extension can subscribe to onTabUpdated and exfiltrate users鈥?browsing URLs, resulting in sensitive information disclosure and remote tracking.

This code contains a double free during index parsing caused by incorrect error propagation from read_entry. In the loop that processes entries, parse_index calls read_entry with the untrusted buffer and only treats an entry as invalid if the returned size is zero, so when read_entry hits an error and frees the entry but mistakenly returns a nonzero size, parse_index believes the entry is valid and stores the freed pointer. Subsequent failures or cleanup will free the same memory again, since the vector retains the pointer, which can be reliably triggered by a crafted repository index that forces read_entry onto the faulty error path. The result is a crash and denial of service and in some environments potential memory corruption.

The function lexer_process_char_literal in JerryScript 1.0 is vulnerable to a denial of service due to a NULL pointer dereference when handling empty string literals with escapes. The root cause is that the code allocates a heap block even when the computed length is zero under the has_escape branch and stores the result without checking for NULL, instead of skipping allocation for empty strings. An attacker can supply malformed JavaScript that yields an empty literal after escape processing, which leads the code to request a zero size allocation, store a NULL pointer in the literal structure, and later pass it to the heap free routine which dereferences NULL. This control flow from the has_escape path to zero size allocation and then to deferred free causes an application crash, enabling remote denial of service.

The function ih264d_mark_err_slice_skip in libavc contains a memory safety flaw that can corrupt memory during error slice handling. The root cause is unchecked pointer arithmetic that selects ps_cur_mb_info as "ps_dec->ps_nmb_info + ps_dec->u4_num_mbs_prev_nmb - 1" when u1_num_mbs equals zero and u1_separate_parse equals zero, which underflows to an address before the array if u4_num_mbs_prev_nmb is zero. A crafted H.264 bitstream can drive the decoder into this path after slice header processing, causing an immediate dereference of the invalid ps_cur_mb_info to read fields such as u2_mby and u2_mbx, thereby propagating corrupted state into subsequent macroblock processing and deblocking. This faulty data and control flow aligns with the Android advisory describing memory corruption in Mediaserver and can enable remote code execution within the Mediaserver process.

The vulnerability is a return value misinterpretation in QEMU鈥檚 IDE DMA path where ide_dma_cb calls prepare_buf and treats the condition "if prepare_buf(...) == 0" as a clean end of transfer. The root cause is inconsistent semantics between the IDE core and the BMDMA or AHCI backends, which may return 0 when a guest supplied PRDT describes zero complete sectors rather than signaling a true end of transfer. A malicious guest can craft such a PRDT so that the callback, using the s object from the opaque parameter to reach s->bus->dma->ops->prepare_buf, repeatedly takes the wrong control path and makes no forward progress while the DMA engine continues to drive the request. This leads to an infinite loop, unbounded memory consumption, and eventual host crash.

The vulnerability is an off by one error in FFmpeg used by Chrome that leads to a zero size allocation during media parsing, which can corrupt the heap. It occurs because a bounds miscalculation in handling untrusted video metadata yields an allocation size of zero while later decoding logic proceeds to write the expected number of bytes into that buffer. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted video that drives the miscount path when the browser attempts to decode or demux it. The media pipeline鈥檚 control flow computes buffer sizes from attacker controlled fields, allocates an undersized or zero length buffer, then performs writes based on the intended element count, enabling heap corruption that can cause a crash or potentially allow remote code execution.

The code contains a logic flaw that allows credential poisoning of the primary account during processing of a Dice signout header. When a listed account matches the primary account and the consistency mode is kDice, the handler calls UpdateCredentials with kInvalidRefreshToken instead of revoking the credentials, in contrast to secondary accounts which use RevokeCredentials. Because the list of signed out accounts is derived from header controlled account_infos, an attacker who can cause the browser to process a crafted signout header can trigger the path where signed_out_account equals the primary account. The data and control flow from account_infos through PickAccountIdForAccount to the equality check drive execution to UpdateCredentials which overwrites the refresh token with an invalid sentinel while keeping the account state, creating an inconsistent and corrupted sign in state. The impact is a forced logout and denial of service against the primary account along with persistent account state confusion until the user reauthenticates.

Vulnerable description: The vulnerability is a fail open misclassification in Chrome鈥檚 download protection where the constructor initializes the flag with "zipped_executable_(false)" causing archives that contain executables to be treated as non archives. It occurs because the flag is set unconditionally during construction and is not derived from the actual download item, so early checks or error paths that consult this flag can proceed under a false assumption. An attacker can trigger this by inducing code paths that read the flag before archive detection completes or by causing detection to fail, which leaves the flag at its insecure default. The data and control flow shows the flag鈥檚 value is tied only to constructor entry and parameters rather than content analysis, so downstream logic may skip stricter checks for archives. As a result an attacker can reduce download scrutiny and facilitate delivery of dangerous executables, contributing to bypass of sandbox protections after renderer compromise as described by the CVE.

An integer overflow in snd_compr_allocate_buffer in the ALSA compress offload path allows a local user to cause insufficient buffer allocation and memory corruption. The function computes "buffer_size = fragment_size * fragments" with no bounds check and these values are user controlled via the SNDRV_COMPRESS_SET_PARAMS ioctl. The overflowed buffer_size is then passed to kmalloc while the original fragment_size and fragments are stored in the runtime state or, when ops->copy is set, a NULL buffer is recorded with the large unvalidated sizes, which enables later read or write operations to overrun the allocated memory or dereference NULL. An attacker can craft parameter values that force wraparound, leading to kernel crashes and denial of service with potential for further unspecified impact.

The code is vulnerable because it sets 鈥渋nfo.fMask = SEE_MASK_NOASYNC | SEE_MASK_FLAG_NO_UI鈥?when invoking ShellExecuteEx to open a microsoft-edge protocol URL, which suppresses OS security UI and checks. The root cause is the inappropriate use of the NO_UI flag while processing potentially untrusted input. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted url that is concatenated into 鈥渕icrosoft-edge:鈥?and written into the SHELLEXECUTEINFO structure, after which ShellExecuteEx executes the external handler without prompting. This data flow from the untrusted parameter into the protocol URL, combined with the NO_UI execution mode, enables silent navigation or file downloads and can bypass OS malware checks, resulting in user consent bypass and potential code execution paths through the protocol handler.

The function setCompositionTimeToSampleParams in SampleTable contains an integer overflow that leads to a heap buffer overflow when parsing the composition time to sample table. The root cause is that an untrusted entry count read from the file is used in unchecked arithmetic for size validation, allocation, and iteration, for example comparing data_size to numEntries plus 1 times 8, allocating new uint32_t of length 2 times numEntries, and reading numEntries times 8 bytes. An attacker can craft a media file with a very large numEntries so these products wrap on 32 bit platforms, making the size check succeed while the allocated buffer is too small and the subsequent read and loop over 2 times numEntries proceed. This mismatch causes out of bounds writes during the ntohl normalization loop, enabling heap corruption, denial of service, or potential remote code execution when the malformed file is processed.

The function ft_bitmap_assure_buffer contains an integer signedness bug that can lead to integer overflow and a heap based buffer overflow. It declares width and height as FT_Int in "FT_Int i, width, height" then assigns them from unsigned bitmap fields, so large values from PNG derived rows or pitch can wrap to negative and corrupt calculations of new_pitch and len. An attacker can embed a crafted PNG inside a TrueType font that provides oversized rows or pitch which the Load_SBit_Png path in FreeType before 2.5.4 fails to restrict, causing this function to compute a small allocation with FT_QALLOC_MULT but perform a larger copy using FT_MEM_COPY based on the tainted values. The resulting under allocation followed by copy overruns the heap leading to denial of service and potentially arbitrary code execution.

The perf_event_interrupt handler on PowerPC contains an integer handling flaw in its overflow detection for performance counters. A counter value read as an unsigned long is truncated and interpreted as a signed int for a negative test, which misdetects wrap events and can cause the code to miss the need to record and restart the counter. A local user can configure perf events to drive counters into these states, leading the handler to skip proper servicing and leaving the performance monitor overflow unhandled. Since the value from read_pmc feeds directly into this flawed decision, the PMU interrupt can retrigger continuously, resulting in an unhandled performance monitor exception and a kernel denial of service.

The code contains a race condition in the audio output device constructor that can lead to memory corruption and code execution. The root cause is the unsynchronized shared state flag initialized as "is_started_(false)" being accessed across threads while a new audio thread is created and published during construction via "audio_thread_(new AudioDeviceThread())". An attacker can trigger the race by driving rapid audio start and stop or initialization sequences through IPC, causing concurrent reads and writes of the start state between the IO thread and the audio thread. This unsafe publication and racy lifecycle management desynchronize control flow around stream creation and callbacks, enabling use after free of audio objects and ultimately allowing remote code execution as described by the CVE.

The function krb5_gss_process_context_token is vulnerable to use after free and double free because it does not properly maintain the security context handle. After processing a delete context token through kg_unseal, it calls krb5_gss_delete_sec_context using the address of the local copy of the handle, which does not clear the caller鈥檚 handle and can attempt to free the context a second time. An attacker can trigger this by sending crafted GSSAPI traffic such as to kadmind, leaving the caller with a dangling handle that is later dereferenced at the check 鈥渋f !ctx->established鈥?or re freed, causing memory corruption. This flaw enables reliable daemon crashes and may allow arbitrary code execution through exploitation of the stale pointer.

The code is vulnerable to an out of bounds read due to unguarded indexing of a potentially empty vector. The root cause is reliance on non fatal EXPECT checks that do not halt execution combined with unconditional dereference of entry_records[0] in the statement "EXPECT_EQ(AppCacheEntry::MASTER, entry_records[0].flags)" after a size expectation and a conditional erase that can remove the first element. An attacker controlled or unexpected database state where FindEntriesForCache fails or returns an entry ordering that triggers the erase can leave entry_records empty and still lead to the dereference. Because control flow proceeds despite failed expectations, the code attempts to access an element that does not exist, which can result in a crash or undefined behavior and enable denial of service.

KioskNextHomeInterfaceBrokerImpl::KioskNextHomeInterfaceBrokerImpl(
content::BrowserContext* context)
: connector_(content::BrowserContext::GetConnectorFor(context)->Clone()),
app_controller_(std::make_unique<AppControllerImpl>(

Vulnerable description: This constructor exposes a lifetime vulnerability by accepting a raw "content::BrowserContext* context" and immediately using it without validation, which can lead to a use after free or null dereference. The root cause is the API boundary trusting a pointer whose lifetime is not guaranteed and then invoking "GetConnectorFor(context)->Clone()" and "Profile::FromBrowserContext(context)" in the initializer list with no checks. If a caller supplies a null or stale context such as one that has already been destroyed, the data flow from the parameter directly into these dereferences triggers access to freed memory. This flaw mirrors the class of heap use after free issues described in the PDFium CVE and could result in a crash, heap corruption, or potentially code execution if an attacker can influence object lifetime.

An information disclosure flaw exists in acpi_ps_complete_final_op in drivers acpi acpica psobject.c where the function fails to flush the node and node_ext caches before returning on completion or error paths. The root cause is that early exits controlled by the auxiliary variable Status2 after checks like ACPI_FAILURE and calls such as AcpiPsCompleteThisOp allow the function to terminate without clearing these caches. A crafted ACPI table can drive the AML parsing state machine via AscendingCallback to produce failure or terminate conditions that steer control flow into these unflushed return paths. As a result stale cached objects can be emitted in a kernel stack dump revealing kernel stack contents and pointers which enables local attackers to obtain sensitive information and to bypass KASLR on kernels through 4.9 with broader information leakage through 4.12.9.

The function PulseAudioMixer::GetAudioInfo is vulnerable because it casts away constness of this via const_cast to a non const PulseAudioMixer pointer and exposes that pointer to an asynchronous callback. The root cause is a violation of const correctness combined with reliance on a debug only DCHECK for locking which provides no synchronization in release builds. The flaw is triggered when GetAudioInfo is called on a const or shared instance and the mutable this pointer is embedded in the CallbackWrapper and passed through pa_context_get_sink_info_by_index to the callback which may modify object state. This data and control flow breaks the immutability guarantee and allows the callback to mutate shared fields without proper locking leading to data races undefined behavior and state corruption. An attacker who can cause concurrent or reentrant calls to this API can induce crashes denial of service or unauthorized manipulation of mixer state.

The vulnerability is a lack of recursion prevention in the Linux sound high resolution timer callback that allows re entry into the timer code path and leads to deadlock. The root cause is missing synchronization and cancellation between user controlled ioctl operations and the hrtimer callback, exemplified by a stop routine that merely clears a running flag with atomic_set but does not cancel or serialize against in flight callbacks. A local user can issue a crafted sequence of ioctls to invoke start or stop while the callback is executing, causing the control path to re enter the same code while locks are held. Without a happens before guarantee or a recursion guard, this re entry can deadlock the audio timer subsystem and yield a reliable kernel denial of service.

The vulnerability arises from defining the sBIT value for 16 to 8 scaling as an internal gamma bound, implemented as "# define SBIT_16_TO_8 PNG_MAX_GAMMA_8", which defaults to 11 and exceeds the valid range for 8 bit output. This occurs because the preprocessor condition sets PNG_MAX_GAMMA_8 to 11 when not predefined, and the alias is then passed through to gamma processing without validation, causing downstream code that assumes sBIT is at most 8 to miscompute shifts, table indexes, or buffer sizes. An attacker can trigger the flaw by supplying a crafted image that forces the 16 to 8 gamma scaling path so that the out of range sBIT propagates through gamma_transform_test and related routines. The resulting logic and memory errors can corrupt process memory during image decoding, enabling privilege escalation as reflected by the CVE affecting Android builds using vulnerable libpng versions.

The code contains an information disclosure vulnerability by logging sensitive operational metadata. The root cause is the use of LOG(WARNING) to emit exact changestamp values without sanitization or restriction to debug-only logging. It is triggered after a successful fetch of the AboutResource when the comparison shows the local changestamp is greater than the remote, causing the message "Local resource metadata is fresher than server, local = ... , server = ..." to be printed with both values. The data and control flow use the server provided largest_change_id and the function input local_changestamp to decide the branch and then pass these values directly into the logging sink. An attacker with access to production logs can infer synchronization state and operational timing, which can aid profiling, targeted probing, and facilitate further attacks.

The code is vulnerable because it builds a single entry DMA scatterlist from an arbitrary buffer using sg_init_one in an environment where CONFIG_VMAP_STACK can place stack buffers across noncontiguous virtual pages. The root cause is the assumption implied by struct scatterlist sg[1] and sg_init_one(sg, buf, count) that buf is virtually and DMA contiguously addressable, which is false for vmapped kernel stacks that may require multiple scatterlist segments. A local user can trigger the flaw by reaching this path with a stack resident buffer that spans more than one vmapped page, at which point buf and count flow directly into sg_init_one and then to __send_to_port without copying to DMA safe memory or constructing a multi entry scatterlist. The result is incorrect DMA mapping and I O that can corrupt memory or crash the system and may enable other unspecified impact.

The code is vulnerable to a crash caused by insufficient checks for short PNG files. After opening the blob, it only verifies the 8 byte PNG signature with the guard "if count < 8" and then immediately calls ReadOnePNGImage without ensuring that subsequent PNG chunks are present or that enough data remains. A crafted truncated PNG that retains a valid header can therefore pass this gate and drive the downstream parser into short reads and invalid memory access during chunk processing. This control flow from minimal header validation to unguarded deep parsing enables an attacker to trigger a process crash and achieve denial of service.

Poppler before version 0.22.1 contains an invalid memory access vulnerability in Splash vertFlipImage. The function declares pointers p0 and p1 but never initializes them to a valid image buffer and uses memcpy with a copy length based on width rather than the full row size width times nComps, creating a mismatch between allocation and copy operations. An attacker can craft a PDF with chosen image dimensions and component counts so that the function allocates a line buffer for width times nComps yet performs memcpy from and to uninitialized addresses while iterating with expressions like p0 += width and p1 -= width, which leads to out of bounds reads and writes. This flawed data and control flow results in memory corruption, enabling denial of service and potentially arbitrary code execution.

The code is vulnerable because parse_object dereferences attacker controlled input immediately with the check "if *value != '{'" and then proceeds to parse strings from the same untrusted buffer. The root cause is the lack of pointer and length validation at entry combined with a flaw in parse_string that mishandles UTF8 and Unicode escape sequences by accepting a non hex character after a backslash u and writing past heap bounds. An attacker can trigger the issue by supplying a crafted JSON object whose field names or values contain malformed escape sequences that flow through skip and into parse_string. This data and control flow lets the heap based overflow occur during string parsing, which can crash the process or enable arbitrary code execution.

The xlnx.xps-ethernetlite receive callback in QEMU contains a heap based buffer overflow when copying incoming packet data into the emulated RX buffer without validating the packet length. The root cause is that the attacker controlled size value is used directly as the copy length into the heap allocated regs array at an offset derived from rxbase, with no check that size fits within the per buffer capacity of roughly 0x800 bytes. An attacker can trigger this by sending an oversized EthernetLite frame that passes the minimal control checks, after which the code reads header bytes and then copies size bytes into the RX buffer, causing a write past the end of the allocated region. This uncontrolled write corrupts heap memory in the QEMU process and can lead to a crash or arbitrary code execution on the host.

The set_config function in the Qualcomm video decoder mishandles untrusted configuration data, leading to heap memory corruption in mediaserver. The root cause is the use of attacker controlled lengths and pointer derived values without validation, for example computing m_vendor_config.nDataSize as config->nDataSize minus 6 minus 1 plus extra_size which can underflow, deriving nal_length from config->pData at offset 4, and copying len bytes from pSrcBuf into pDestBuf with no bounds checks. An attacker can trigger this by passing a crafted blob through OMX IndexVendorVideoExtraData that sets a too small nDataSize or inflates the parsed NAL lengths, causing out of bounds reads and writes or a null dereference after an unchecked malloc. This unsafe data and control flow allows writes past allocated buffers inside mediaserver and enables elevation of privilege up to Signature or SignatureOrSystem as described by the CVE.

The bmexec_trans function in grep 2.19 through 2.21 contains an out of bounds heap read that can cause a crash when -F is used with crafted input. The root cause is unchecked signed integer arithmetic on len taken from kwset->mind which is an int and is multiplied as 12 * len and 11 * len to drive control flow and compute bounds. A large len can overflow these expressions so the condition "size > 12 * len" and the calculation "ep = text + size - 11 * len" become wrong, after which the unrolled loop advances tp and dereferences U(tp[-1]) or calls memchr_kwset with an excessive length beyond the end of the buffer. This corrupted data and control flow leads the search routine to read past allocated memory resulting in denial of service.

The vulnerability is a NULL pointer dereference in ssl23_get_client_hello that occurs when the function mishandles an unexpected handshake that uses a protocol the server has disabled. The root cause is inconsistent version negotiation and error handling that can transition into SSL3 or TLS specific processing without ensuring the corresponding state is initialized when the client proposes an unsupported protocol. An attacker can trigger it by sending an SSLv3 ClientHello to a server configured with NO SSLv3 which after the CVE 2014 3568 changes can lead the code to proceed into SSL23_ST_SR_CLNT_HELLO_B and invoke operations like ssl3_finish_mac or message callbacks that assume SSL3 state, causing a NULL dereference. The impact is a remote denial of service through a daemon crash.

The code contains an out of bounds memory access in touchEvent due to a mismatch between the loop bound and the container being indexed. It iterates with "for (unsigned i = 0; i < event.m_points.size(); i++)" but writes into "tEvent.m_points[i]" without ensuring that tEvent.m_points is at least as large as event.m_points, so any divergence after copying or filtering causes invalid writes. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a crafted document that drives the input pipeline to produce a TouchEvent where the number of points in event and its copy diverge, making the loop write past the end of tEvent.m_points. Since the loop count is derived from attacker influenced event data and the body updates tEvent fields, this leads to memory corruption with outcomes ranging from crashes to potential remote code execution, consistent with the CVE description of issues exploitable via a crafted document.

The vulnerability is a denial of service in QEMU USB OHCI emulation before version 2.9.0 caused by an infinite loop due to an incorrect return value in the function ohci_service_iso_td. The root cause is that on certain invalid TD conditions the function returns 1 after checks like bad cc not accessed and exits without advancing the ED head or completing the TD, which leaves the same descriptor to be processed again. A malicious guest can craft isochronous TD fields such as the starting frame, frame count, and the per frame offset condition codes so that the code path that sets an error condition is taken and then returns 1, effectively instructing the scheduler to retry the same TD indefinitely. Because relative frame number and offset condition codes are derived from guest controlled memory and the control flow neither updates the queue state nor retires the TD, the OHCI schedule spins on the same descriptor and the attacker can hang the emulation thread, resulting in a denial of service.

Blink mishandles same origin enforcement when a media element source changes, allowing a remote page to bypass the same origin policy in Chrome before version 68. The root cause is that OnCurrentSrcChanged bases its CORS decision on the caller supplied reference parameter "const KURL& current_src" rather than an authoritative resolved origin, so policy is applied to attacker influenced URL state. An attacker can trigger this by serving a crafted page that sets the media source with redirects or rapid changes so that the check observes a benign URL while the resource ultimately resolves cross origin. In the function the untrusted "current_src" flows directly into "PassesCurrentSrcCORSAccessCheck(current_src)" and the result updates "passes_current_src_cors_access_check_" which governs access, allowing the decision to be made on the wrong origin.
