Successful exploitation can expose cross origin media to the WebAudio pipeline or other consumers and thereby bypass the same origin policy.

The read_image_tga function is vulnerable to an out of bounds read when parsing RLE encoded TGA images, leading to denial of service. The root cause is that the decoder assumes the compressed input length equals the uncompressed image size by reading exactly image_block_size bytes, then expands RLE data without validating input bounds, so expressions like tga->bitmap[bitmap_caret] = decompression_buffer[buffer_caret + j] can read past decompression_buffer. An attacker can craft RLE control bytes that set encoded_pixels and advance buffer_caret in a way that the inner expansion loops request more source bytes than were provided. The data flow from tga->bits to pixel_block_size and image_block_size drives allocations and loop limits, but since buffer_caret and buffer_caret plus pixel_block_size are never checked against the actual available input, malformed packets trigger out of range reads. This allows a remote attacker to crash an application using libgd by supplying a crafted TGA file.

The code is vulnerable to a use after free caused by reading selection state during a node removal event. In NodeWillBeRemoved the builder preserves handle visibility via SetIsHandleVisible(selection_.IsHandleVisible()) after only checking that the selection is not none, which allows the visibility query to dereference selection internals that may already reference the node being removed. This is triggered when a selection base or extent targets the soon to be removed node and a malicious page or input causes that node to be removed while the selection remains active, causing IsHandleVisible to traverse stale pointers. Because execution of the visibility read is control dependent on the non empty selection check and occurs within the removal callback, the code can read freed memory leading to crashes and potentially exploitable memory corruption.

The vulnerability is a denial of service in the Linux perf subsystem where overflows of the software CPU clock event are mishandled in the interrupt handler. The root cause is that the overflow path invokes record_and_restart on the overflowing event without correctly acknowledging or clearing the software overflow condition, which immediately retriggers the same path. As perf_event_interrupt iterates over counters, reads a value, treats a negative value as overflow, and then calls record_and_restart with the event and regs from interrupt context, the condition persists for PERF_COUNT_SW_CPU_CLOCK so the handler fires repeatedly and livelocks the CPU. A local user can create a crafted perf event with a very small period for the software CPU clock to trigger relentless interrupts and hang the system.

The code that parses IPv6 Hop by Hop and Destination Options in DecodeIPV6ExtHdrs is vulnerable to misparsing that can lead to denial of service and signature detection bypass. The root cause is an off by one bounds check that validates option length using offset plus one plus ip6_optlen while later reading option data starting at pointer plus two, combined with a failure to advance the pointer and offset for non PAD1 options. An attacker can craft IPv6 options so that the check passes while the subsequent read oversteps the available buffer or so that the loop never progresses, for example by selecting these extension headers via the next header value and controlling the extension length and per option ip6_optlen. In the internal flow optslen is derived from the extension header length, the loop consumes options based on ip6_optlen, and the arithmetic error and missing increments allow an out of bounds read or an infinite loop, preventing traversal to the transport protocol decoder. As a result Suricata can crash or stall and application layer detection such as DNS may never be invoked, enabling evasion consistent with the reported issue fixed in version 4.1.2.

The function is vulnerable to iterator invalidation and data race because it reads and writes touch point state after dispatching an event that may reenter and mutate the same container. After copying points and calling page()->touchEvent(event), the code checks and updates each element using the condition "if it->m_state != TouchReleased" without any synchronization or defensive copy, so the iterator or the referenced element can be invalid if the dispatch modified touches. The control flow proceeds directly from function entry to this check with no barrier or lock, allowing a crafted input to drive event handling that mutates touches during or immediately after dispatch. An attacker can exploit this through malicious content such as a crafted document to induce memory safety violations leading to crashes or potentially arbitrary code execution.

The code is vulnerable to unbounded blocking connections in the remote CIB listener, enabling denial of service. The root cause is a flawed timeout check in the authentication wait loop that compares start minus now to a small threshold, which remains true as time advances, so the loop never terminates while the socket is blocking. An attacker can simply connect and send no login message, causing the loop to repeatedly receive and sleep while the loop counter lpc increases but is not used to enforce any limit. This control flow holds the connection open indefinitely and allows many such connections to exhaust file descriptors and processing slots, resulting in service unavailability.

The vulnerability is a denial of service in tcpdump print-wb.c within wb_prep where an inverted bounds check allows out of bounds reads that crash the process. The root cause is a loop condition that negates the ND_TTEST check so the code continues precisely when there is not enough captured data for the pgstate structure. An attacker can craft a packet whose pp_n and related fields cause the parser to enter the loop with insufficient data, after which the code dereferences ps and iterates into io entries derived from untrusted input. Because n and ps come from the packet and the decision to iterate relies on the flawed check against the capture boundary, the control flow drives pointer advancement beyond the buffer, resulting in a segmentation fault and a reliable crash in versions before 4.7.4.

The vulnerability is a platform guard flaw where the only functional body of GraphicsContext::clip is compiled under the directive "#ifdef __WXMAC__", while other builds fall through to "notImplemented", leaving a core painting primitive absent. The root cause is conditional compilation that removes a valid clipping implementation on non macOS targets, creating an unsafe fallback that can abort or leave rendering state inconsistent. It can be triggered by crafted web content that exercises clipping during layout and painting, such as sequences involving floating styles, which call clip expecting a valid clipping region. Because all control flow in this function depends on the macro gate, non macOS builds bypass path setup and state management, enabling denial of service and in the broader rendering pipeline potentially facilitating use after free as observed in the CVE.

The vulnerability is a use after free in PDFium formfiller caused by improper tracking of the lifetime of IPWL_FocusHandler and IPWL_Provider objects. It arises because the formfiller retains references to these objects after they are destroyed, so later focus or provider callbacks dereference freed memory. An attacker can trigger this by delivering a crafted PDF that exercises form interactions when rendered, for example when code navigates a WebContents to such a resource using "NavigateAndCommit". This faulty control and data flow leads event processing to touch dangling pointers, enabling renderer crashes and potentially arbitrary code execution.

The code is vulnerable to a null pointer dereference in ExternalFeedbackReporterAndroid::ReportExternalFeedback because it assumes that objects obtained from WebContents are always valid. The root cause is reliance on DCHECK rather than runtime validation after obtaining the helper with "WindowAndroidHelper* helper =" and the window via "helper->GetWindowAndroid()". An attacker can trigger this by causing a state where WebContents is valid but has no associated WindowAndroidHelper or where the window has been detached, leading these calls to return null. The control flow proceeds to dereference these pointers and invoke "window->GetJavaObject()" for a JNI call, and since the DCHECKs do not execute in release builds, a null pointer is accessed. The impact is a process crash resulting in denial of service.

The vulnerability is weak DNS query entropy that allows cache poisoning in the resolver. It occurs because the code uses a global UDP control block "static struct udp_pcb *dns_pcb" which fixes or greatly stabilizes the source port across queries and pairs it with predictable identifiers such as a sequential dns_seqno rather than random values. An attacker can trigger it by racing a spoofed DNS reply that guesses the stable source port and the predictable ID and having it arrive before the legitimate response. The internal flow relies on the shared pcb for packet emission and on deterministic ID generation, so functions that build and send queries inherit this predictability and repeatedly expose the same port and easily guessed IDs. Successful exploitation lets an attacker inject forged DNS records into the resolver cache, redirecting victims to attacker controlled hosts and enabling traffic interception or redirection.

The function CancelHandwritingStrokes is vulnerable because it forwards the caller supplied stroke_count to the Chrome OS cancel handwriting API without validating sign or bounds. The root cause is missing input validation, as the code only checks initialization and then passes stroke_count unchanged to the callee. Data and control flow show the parameter originates at function entry and reaches the call without constraints, so crafted PDF content with nested functions can drive an out of range or negative count into this path. Consistent with the Chrome CVE on improper handling of nested functions in PDFs, this can cause a denial of service through a crash and may enable other unspecified impact if the callee mismanages the invalid value.

The code is vulnerable because it accepts an untyped pointer in the parameter "void* object" and immediately performs a blind cast to "InputMethodLibraryImpl*" before dereferencing it, with no validation of type, nullness, or lifetime. The root cause is unchecked pointer use in a callback that is only gated by a UI thread check, which does not protect against stale or freed objects. In the scenario described by the CVE, a crafted PDF that triggers improperly handled nested functions can cause reentrant control flow that invalidates the expected object and leads this handler to operate on invalid memory. Since the object parameter flows directly into the static cast and subsequent method invocation to change the current input method, an attacker can trigger a crash and potentially achieve unspecified further impact.

The code contains a use after free in the media timeline event handler because the early return for mouseover, mouseout, and mousemove is placed after invoking the base default event handler, which can execute script and destroy or detach the element. The root cause is an ordering bug combined with the absence of a liveness check after the reentrant call, so the object may be freed while subsequent logic still accesses media controls and layout objects. An attacker can trigger this by generating left button mouse events on the control while page script hooked by the base handler removes the control during scrubbing or input handling. The control flow accepts the event, calls the base handler which may free the element, then continues to compute time and access the slider and media controls, resulting in dereferencing freed memory with potential crash or code execution.

The function opj_pi_next_rpcl in OpenJPEG before 2.2.0 contains a division by zero that remote attackers can trigger with crafted J2K input. The iterator computes step sizes pi->dx and pi->dy from component and resolution parameters using left shifts such as comp->dx << rpx and comp->dy << rpy but never verifies they are nonzero. If initialization is skipped due to the pi->first flag or if the computed steps resolve to zero, the nested loops advance y and x using dy minus y % dy and dx minus x % dx which performs a modulo with a zero divisor. By selecting resolution and tiling values that yield zero step sizes or prevent proper initialization, an attacker can force this path and crash the decoder, causing denial of service.

The code is vulnerable to double free or use after free due to unsafe lifetime management of a raw callback pointer. The root cause is ambiguous ownership combined with calling the callback and then unconditionally performing delete callback, with no guarantee that the callback remains valid after invocation. An attacker can trigger this by providing a callback that self deletes during its Run method or that causes the callback to be freed indirectly through reentrant teardown paths, after which the unconditional delete operates on already freed memory. The sequential control flow computes a status, calls the callback, then deletes it without any guard, which can lead to memory corruption, application crashes, or potential code execution.

The function xsltAddTemplate is vulnerable because it only checks that style, cur, and cur->match are non null and does not verify their validity or coherence with the stylesheet state. An attacker can supply a crafted XSLT that abuses namespace nodes so these fields are non null yet dangling or malformed. After this weak guard the code immediately dereferences cur and feeds cur->match and style->doc into the pattern compiler and later uses the compiled pattern as if it had a valid first step, which can drive control and data flow into out of bounds heap memory access. This enables denial of service and possibly other impacts consistent with the reported libxslt issue involving mishandled namespace nodes.

The function is vulnerable to a heap buffer overflow when processing untrusted EMF images. It reads EMF width and height and assigns them to size_t image columns and rows without validating range, then truncates these values to 32 bit LONG when filling the BITMAPINFOHEADER for CreateDIBSection which allocates the pixel buffer, creating a mismatch between allocation and use. An attacker can supply an EMF with extremely large or negative logical dimensions that convert to huge size_t values while the GDI allocation is based on truncated LONG values, so the loops that iterate over image rows and columns write past the end of ppBits. This overflow corrupts heap memory and can cause a crash and potentially enable remote code execution.

The virtqueue_map_desc function in QEMU contains a denial of service vulnerability caused by an infinite loop when processing a descriptor that yields a zero length mapping. Inside the loop the code sets len via cpu_physical_memory_map and decrements the remaining size with "sz -= len" under the condition "while (sz)" but it never validates that len is greater than zero, nor does it enforce an in loop bound on the iov and addr indices. A malicious guest can supply a descriptor that results in len equal to zero, which leaves sz unchanged and causes the loop to spin indefinitely while continually incrementing num_sg and writing iov[num_sg] and addr[num_sg]. This leads to a hang and can crash the QEMU process, enabling a local guest to cause a denial of service.

The vulnerability is a race condition in l2tp_ip6_bind where the code checks the socket state using the line "if (!sock_flag(sk, SOCK_ZAPPED))" before taking the per socket lock. The root cause is that this state check is performed on shared socket state without synchronization which creates a time of check to time of use window. An attacker can trigger it by issuing multiple concurrent bind calls on the same L2TPv3 IPv6 socket so that each call observes the socket as zapped and proceeds into the binding path. Because control flow depends on the unsynchronized check the threads can both modify bind tables and reset flags leading to inconsistent state and potential use after free. The impact is local denial of service and possible privilege escalation as described for this class of bugs in the L2TPv3 IP encapsulation code paths.

This code contains an out of bounds read that can crash the MiniSSDPd daemon when processing search requests. The root cause is that a user supplied length is decoded into l and then used directly as the third argument of a binary comparison against internal header buffers without verifying that l is nonnegative and no larger than those buffers. An attacker can send a crafted request with a negative or oversized length that passes the input buffer bounds check yet forces memcmp on device header fields to read far beyond their ends. The data flows from the socket into buf, then type, p, and l are derived, and in the SEARCH paths l and p are used directly in comparisons against d headers without constraining l to the corresponding header length, enabling a local user to trigger a daemon crash via out of bounds memory access.

The code is vulnerable to a use after free in the IPv6 transmit path before Linux 4.3.3. In tcp_v6_send_synack the call to "ip6_xmit(sk, skb, fl6, np->opt, np->tclass)" passes the IPv6 options pointer from the socket without any locking or reference protection, so that options modified via crafted sendmsg ancillary data or sticky option updates can be freed or replaced concurrently. Data and control flow show that np and thus np->opt originate from the input socket and are consumed directly at transmit time, with line dependencies from the function arguments to the ip6_xmit call leaving the lifetime of np->opt unsynchronized. A local attacker can trigger this race to cause dereference of freed options memory, leading to kernel crash or potentially escalation of privileges.

The code is vulnerable to an out of bounds read because a byte buffer is reinterpreted as an array of a wider Type and then indexed using a byte count. The root cause is the unsafe cast at the line that performs reinterpret cast from uint8 pointer to Type pointer combined with treating length as a count of Type elements rather than bytes, which also risks misalignment and violates effective type rules. The issue is triggered when the algorithm is not muted and the loop reads output at indices from zero to length, causing reads past the end of the buffer for non byte sized Type values. Data and control flow from the function parameters into the cast and then into the loop bound and the dereference ensures that a crafted media buffer and length pairing can force the invalid access, as seen in scenarios involving media seek operations. An attacker can cause a process crash and denial of service by supplying input that induces this over read.

The vulnerability is incorrect enforcement of Content Security Policy during navigations, allowing a window where the new document begins loading without CSP applied. It occurs because the code sets the document to the Loading state before installing CSP, then transfers ownership with content_security_policy_.Release() to InitContentSecurityPolicy, so policy adoption happens after loading is already signaled. An attacker can trigger this by navigating a user to a crafted HTML page that initiates subresource requests or script execution immediately upon document creation, before CSP has been initialized. The control flow shows that InitContentSecurityPolicy is invoked only after SetReadyState is called and a null check passes, enabling actions to proceed without policy, which can lead to CSP bypass and the fetching or execution of content that should be blocked.

The function svc_rdma_sendto contains a vulnerability where it treats an untrusted receive buffer as a fully formed rpcrdma_msg and dereferences it without validation. The root cause is that rdma_argp is set from the first page of the request using "rdma_argp = page_address(rqstp->rq_pages[0])" and then its fields are read and parsed with no check that the buffer is large enough or correctly structured. An attacker can trigger this by sending a malformed or truncated RDMA request so that the page does not contain a complete message, which leads to invalid memory access when the code copies header fields and when helper routines parse write and reply arrays. The resulting invalid dereferences and error paths can crash the kernel or leak resources during repeated failures, enabling denial of service through resource consumption.

The vulnerability is the acceptance of a security relevant parameter without any validation or use, specifically the "sessionId" argument in DownmixLib_Create, which permits effect instances to be created irrespective of caller session constraints. This occurs because the function signature introduces sessionId yet no data or control flow within the body references it, so creation proceeds unconditionally to allocate and initialize the effect module and return a handle. An attacker can trigger this by invoking effect creation with arbitrary or privileged looking session identifiers, thereby obtaining effect instances in unintended contexts and reaching libeffects code paths. In combination with the heap based buffer overflows documented for libeffects in the referenced CVE, this missing session binding broadens the attack surface and can facilitate arbitrary code execution by allowing crafted applications to reach and exercise the vulnerable heap handling logic in mediaserver.

The function implements a heap buffer overflow due to incorrect allocation size calculation. The root cause is an integer overflow when computing the buffer size in the expression "new char[len + 1]" after len is derived from strlen without any bounds checks, which can wrap and produce a too small allocation. An attacker can craft MKV metadata parsed by libwebm in mediaserver so that src is extremely long, the preliminary null checks permit the allocation, and then strcpy copies the full string into the undersized buffer. The control flow only validates pointer presence and destination nullity while the data flows from src to len to allocation to copy without size validation, leading to memory corruption that can crash mediaserver or enable remote code execution.

Psensor鈥檚 embedded web server is vulnerable to directory traversal because the request handler resolves requested files without verifying they remain under the configured web root. The web root is set from user input via the CLI as "server_data.www_dir = strdup(optarg)" and later create_response builds a file path from the HTTP request path but omits canonicalization and a containment check against this base directory. An attacker can send a crafted request containing sequences such as ../ to traverse out of the web directory and retrieve files from elsewhere on the filesystem. This data and control flow enables remote disclosure of arbitrary files and sensitive system information, which can facilitate further compromise.

The vulnerability is a use after free in Chrome鈥檚 Autofill where form field updates can continue to run after JavaScript deletes the hosting frame, leading to dereferences of freed objects. The root cause is fragile lifecycle and state management in the Autofill agent, notably the constructor setting the security relevant flag to 鈥渨as_password_autofilled_(false)鈥?during base observer initialization, which exposes a false autofill state to early update flows and fails to gate or cancel processing when the frame is torn down. An attacker can trigger this by causing an autofill or field update and simultaneously executing script that removes the frame, so the agent鈥檚 update logic proceeds on the not autofilled path and accesses the now freed RenderFrame. This control and data flow yields a crash for denial of service and may enable other impacts depending on the specific stale accesses.

The code is vulnerable to a NULL function pointer dereference in the regset handling path because it enters the note creation block based on the condition "regset->core_note_type" and optional activity but then unconditionally calls "regset->get" without verifying that this callback exists. The root cause is missing validation of mandatory regset operations, as the control flow trusts the user_regset_view contents and uses only the core_note_type and active checks to gate execution. An attacker can trigger this by causing the kernel to process a regset that advertises a core note but lacks a get method during thread core dump generation or through regset based ptrace operations. When this path is taken the call to a NULL "regset->get" crashes the kernel, yielding a reliable local denial of service and potentially enabling other unintended effects depending on configuration.

The code contains an initialization order vulnerability in the Vp9Parser constructor that invokes Reset before the object state is properly established. The root cause is calling a stateful routine during construction without first ensuring members are initialized, so Reset may access or modify uninitialized fields and break class invariants. The control flow from constructor entry to the Reset call and then to function exit guarantees this unsafe sequence occurs every time the object is created. An attacker can trigger this by causing the application to instantiate the parser while handling crafted media, potentially leading to use of uninitialized data, crashes, memory corruption, or even code execution depending on Reset interactions with internal state.

The code in the PHP unserializer contains a heap use after free during cleanup of array elements when processing untrusted serialized data with an invalid element count. The root cause is improper use of the hash API for deletion in the UNDEF cleanup branch, where a string key that was coerced to a numeric index for insertion via the numeric path is later deleted as a string key, causing a mismatch between how the bucket was created and how it is removed. An attacker can craft serialized input with numeric looking string keys and an element count that drives the parser into the UNDEF branch, causing the code to attempt to delete the just inserted slot using the wrong deletion function, leaving stale or unintended buckets while previously scheduled destructors still free memory. This control and data flow inconsistency corrupts the HashTable and can lead to dangling pointers being dereferenced, resulting in memory corruption, crashes, and potential arbitrary code execution, thereby impacting the integrity of PHP.

The code is vulnerable in the Linux and Android path because it returns a raw NetworkChangeNotifierLinux instance without performing required initialization or lifecycle setup. The root cause is that the factory method simply executes 鈥渞eturn new NetworkChangeNotifierLinux();鈥?while other platforms perform explicit startup work, which leaves internal state and callbacks uninitialized. This path is triggered when no custom factory is present, as control flows from the function entry through the factory check to the Linux branch. An attacker who can drive code paths that instantiate and use this improperly initialized notifier can cause crashes, races, or inconsistent network state, leading to denial of service or unreliable behavior in components that depend on network change notifications.

This code path is not vulnerable. The early argument check calls "return V8Proxy::throwNotEnoughArgumentsError();" when the argument count is less than one, which immediately throws an exception and exits before any native object is dereferenced or any reentrant property access occurs. The control flow reaches this line directly from function entry and is influenced only by the argument length, so an attacker can only trigger a benign error rather than affect privileged behavior. This behavior is unrelated to the cited issue in which Chrome failed to require user confirmation for unpacked extension installation and therefore has no security impact.

The function cherokee_validator_ldap_check is vulnerable to authentication bypass when LDAP is used because it does not account for unauthenticated bind semantics with an empty password. The root cause is that the code only validates that the username is non empty via the check using cherokee_buffer_is_empty on the user field but never rejects an empty password before performing the bind. An attacker can trigger this by sending a valid username with an empty password, after which the code builds a filter, performs an LDAP search, extracts the DN, and calls validate_dn with the empty password, which many LDAP servers accept as an anonymous bind that returns success. The control flow then interprets the successful bind as a valid authentication and returns ret_ok, allowing remote attackers to gain access without valid credentials.

The code is vulnerable to type confusion that can lead to an out of bounds read and denial of service. At its root, a generic helper is created with "EntrySyncCallbackHelper::create()" which does not guarantee that the captured result is a directory entry, yet the result is later returned through "helper->getResult" and blindly cast with "static_cast<DirectoryEntrySync*>". An attacker influencing the filesystem operation via a crafted path and options causes "m_fileSystem->getDirectory" to produce a non directory entry, which the generic helper accepts, and subsequent code treats it as a DirectoryEntrySync and reads invalid memory. The data flow from user controlled options into flags and then into the filesystem call makes the helper capture an incompatible object, and the unchecked cast drives the out of bounds read that crashes the process, consistent with the described Chrome denial of service.

The vulnerability is an improper access control in the camera service dump path that allows bypassing the intended permission checks. It occurs because the per client method "CameraDeviceClient::dump" is exposed and executes without routing through "ICameraService::dump," so no signature level authorization is enforced. An attacker can trigger it by invoking the client binder dump entry point directly with crafted arguments, causing the code to call "mFrameProcessor->dump" and "dumpDevice" without validating the caller. This data and control flow lets an unprivileged app coerce mediaserver into performing restricted dump operations, leading to sensitive camera state disclosure and effective elevation to Signature or SignatureOrSystem capabilities.

The function jpc_qmfb_split_colres in the Jasper JPC codec contains a heap buffer overflow caused by under-allocation of a temporary buffer. When numrows is large enough to trigger the heap path, the code allocates buf using only the row-based count as in "jas_alloc2(bufsize, sizeof(jpc_fix_t))" while subsequent operations store m multiplied by numcols elements into this buffer, creating a dimensionality mismatch. An attacker can trigger this by supplying an image that causes bufsize to exceed the small stack threshold and sets numcols greater than one, leading the copy loops to write past the end of the heap allocation. The resulting out of bounds writes can corrupt heap memory, causing crashes or potentially enabling arbitrary code execution.

The code is vulnerable because it uses a deterministically seeded DRBG for blinding during deterministic ECDSA signing, which provides insufficient entropy and leads to repeatable blinding values. The root cause is that p_rng is seeded via mbedtls_hmac_drbg_seed_buf using only data derived from the private key and the message hash, then consumed at the call to ecdsa_sign_restartable with mbedtls_hmac_drbg_random and p_rng, so all randomness becomes a pure function of the key and message. This is triggered when deterministic ECDSA is enabled and a victim signs the same message multiple times, including through the restartable path that preserves the same DRBG state and adds no fresh entropy. As data and control flow from the inputs grp, d, and buf into the seed and then into the RNG used at signing time, the repeated blinding enables side channel averaging, allowing an attacker to recover the private key.

The code is vulnerable because IPv6 Fragment Identification values are not generated per destination, which makes them predictable and reusable across different peers and flows. In ip6_ufo_append_data the function calls ipv6_select_ident and then assigns skb_shinfo skb ip6_frag_id without supplying any destination context, so the ID comes from a destination agnostic generator. An attacker can trigger this by predicting the identification values and injecting crafted fragments that collide with legitimate traffic, causing fragment reassembly confusion or failure. This data flow leads to remote denial of service through disrupted networking, as legitimate packets are dropped or misassembled due to ID collisions.

The vulnerability is an information leak in the media engine that lets a web page infer cross origin data via observable media loading events and state transitions. It occurs because the media element exposes conditional progress signaling based on internal download activity without appropriate same origin or CORS gating or without coarsening the observable behavior. An attacker can trigger it by embedding a cross origin media resource and listening for the presence and timing of the progress event followed by a suspend event as the element switches from loading to idle. The internal logic uses a check of whether loading made progress to decide whether to dispatch progress and then unconditionally dispatches suspend and sets the network state to idle, which exposes whether bytes were received and when, allowing an attacker to deduce cross origin response characteristics and leak information.

The vulnerability is an information disclosure in Blink where iframe Resource Timing data is exposed across navigations, allowing attackers to read timing metrics that should be restricted. It occurs because FrameFetchContext::updateTimingInfoForIFrameNavigation fails to clear or properly gate timing entries with same origin or timing allow origin checks when an iframe navigates and then returns via history navigation, leaving sensitive timing state accessible to the attacker. An attacker can embed an iframe, navigate it to a cross origin page, then trigger history.back so the iframe resumes an attacker controlled context while performance timing entries reflecting the cross origin load remain readable. This flawed data flow lets timing entries persist and be surfaced through the Resource Timing API, enabling attackers to infer sensitive cross origin information such as resource presence, network latency, cache status, or user specific behavior.

The code in usb_parse_configuration performs an out of bounds read that can be triggered by a crafted USB device, leading to a kernel crash and potentially other impacts. The root cause is insufficient validation of input length and descriptor layout, as the function executes "memcpy(&config->desc, buffer, USB_DT_CONFIG_SIZE)" before verifying that the provided size is large enough and then trusts attacker controlled descriptor headers including USB_DT_INTERFACE_ASSOCIATION to drive parsing. An attacker can present a configuration blob that is shorter than the fixed copy size or supply a forged interface association header with a misleading length, causing the parser to advance beyond the valid data. As a result the function reads past the end of the supplied buffer and dereferences invalid memory, producing denial of service and possibly enabling further unspecified effects.

The provided gdAlphaBlend function does not contain a vulnerability; it safely performs per pixel alpha blending and includes guards that prevent division by zero and integer overflow. The potential root cause of a flaw such as a zero divisor or weight overflow is avoided by early returns when src_alpha is "gdAlphaOpaque" or "gdAlphaTransparent" and by computing src_weight as "gdAlphaTransparent - src_alpha" which keeps the final divisor positive. The data flow from src_alpha and dst_alpha ensures tot_weight is at least one before calculating red, green, and blue, and all multiplications and shifts remain within safe 32 bit ranges, so crafted pixel values cannot trigger unsafe arithmetic. Consequently an attacker cannot use this function to cause crashes or memory corruption.

The code in arch s390 ptrace handling is vulnerable because it performs an incorrect validation of user supplied PSW mask bits during PTRACE_POKEUSR_AREA, allowing prohibited address space control bits to be set. The root cause is a flawed check that compares the disallowed portion of the user value against an unmasked constant, which fails to enforce that only permitted bits are present and thus accepts invalid combinations. An attacker can trigger this by supplying an addr that targets regs.psw.mask and a crafted data value via ptrace, where tmp is attacker controlled and the allowed bit mask depends on child state through is_ri_task, causing control flow to enter the psw mask branch and pass the faulty validation. The code then merges the unchecked bits into regs->psw.mask, enabling manipulation of address space selection and granting read and write access to kernel memory, which can be leveraged for privilege escalation.

The function builds a strftime format string from user controlled input and writes the formatted result into mask_decoded5, but in vulnerable versions the destination buffer was not initialized before the call. If the attacker supplies crafted date and time specifiers in the mask so that strftime fails and returns zero, the function proceeds to use mask_decoded5 even though its contents are indeterminate. The data flow runs from the input mask through a series of replacements into mask_decoded4, which is then passed as the format to strftime with mask_decoded5 as the output, and subsequent operations such as lowercasing and logging consume this uninitialized buffer. The root cause is the lack of buffer initialization combined with no check of the strftime return value, which allows a crash and denial of service.

The SUN image reader in ImageMagick before 6.9.0-4 contains an out of bounds read that can be triggered by a crafted SUN file leading to a crash. The root cause is insufficient cross field validation of attacker controlled header values such as width, height, depth, type and length which are used to compute buffer sizes and drive decoding without ensuring the provided data is large enough for the computed image geometry and encoding. An attacker can supply inconsistent values so that the decoder allocates and reads a buffer sized by sun_info.length then proceeds to process more pixels than that buffer contains when handling types like RT_ENCODED or RT_FORMAT_RGB. The data flow is header parse to image geometry and mode selection followed by decoding that iterates over rows and columns using computed sizes that overrun the loaded data resulting in an out of bounds read. The impact is denial of service through application crash when the reader accesses memory past the end of its internal buffer.

The code is vulnerable to buffer over read in the path that copies matched bytes into an arena, leading to crash or information disclosure. The root cause is that match_length is a signed 32 bit value and is increased by untrusted forward_matches without bounds or overflow checks, then used to derive new_match->data_length with no verification that the requested bytes actually reside within the input buffer. An attacker can craft input that makes the regex engine produce a match near the end of the mapped data or that forces the addition to wrap negative, so the copy reads beyond the available data. The data flow goes from args to callback_args to match_length through the statement "match_length += callback_args->forward_matches", then to new_match->data_length and finally into yr_arena_write_data which reads that many bytes from match_data without validating the range. The result is denial of service and possible leakage of adjacent process memory.

The code is vulnerable because it allows installing a new user namespace while the file system state may still be shared, enabling the CLONE_NEWUSER and CLONE_FS combination to create a capability boundary mismatch. The function blocks only when the memory map is shared and requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the target user namespace, but it does not prevent or unshare a shared fs_struct, so commit_creds applies new capabilities while the root directory remains shared with another task. An attacker can trigger this by cloning with CLONE_NEWUSER and CLONE_FS, gaining chroot capability in the new user namespace and then invoking chroot, which due to the shared fs changes the root of the parent or sibling process that did not gain those capabilities. This cross namespace and shared fs condition lets a local user alter the root directory of a more privileged process and thereby escalate privileges.

The handler is vulnerable because it accepts an untyped pointer as "void* object" and immediately casts it to InputMethodLibraryImpl* and uses it without any type, null, or lifetime validation. The root cause is reliance on a raw pointer with only a UI thread check that logs "Not on UI thread" and returns, leaving pointer integrity entirely unchecked. A crafted PDF that abuses nested functions can induce reentrancy or unexpected callback timing so the handler is invoked with a stale or mismatched object, which then flows directly through the cast and into UpdateProperty. This enables type confusion or use after free, producing an application crash and potentially other impact in line with the referenced CVE.

The vulnerability is an integer overflow in ft_smooth_render_generic in smooth ftsmooth.c that miscomputes bitmap dimensions and pitch during subpixel rendering. It occurs because width and height derived from the outline control box are scaled and extended using operations such as width *= 3 and width += 3 * extra with no bounds checks, allowing arithmetic wrap in FT_UInt and FT_Int types. An attacker can trigger it with a crafted font that yields very large outline coordinates or filter extra values so the computed sizes overflow and the allocation or assumed buffer size becomes too small. The internal flow then uses these truncated dimensions in rasterization and in horizontal and vertical replication loops that copy bytes based on width and height, causing writes past the end of the buffer. This leads to memory corruption and can enable arbitrary code execution in applications that render the malicious font.

The code is vulnerable to an out of bounds write during shared memory transfer of print preview data. The root cause is trusting renderer controlled metafile size and content combined with incorrect use of shared memory wrapping in Mojo, where "CopyMetafileDataToSharedMem" and later "mojo::WrapSharedMemoryHandle" can create a mismatch between the allocated mapping and the amount of data copied or expected. An attacker who has compromised the renderer can craft a metafile that passes the minimal non null checks, reach the call to "CopyMetafileDataToSharedMem", set an arbitrary data_size via metafile->GetDataSize, and have this handle and size sent over IPC via PrintHostMsg_DidPreviewPage. Because the copy and handle wrapping depend only on function inputs with no robust bounds or consistency validation, the browser process may write past the end of the shared memory region, resulting in memory corruption that can cause crashes or enable code execution and sandbox escape.

The function hid_copy_transfer_data contains an unsigned length underflow and out of bounds access that can lead to an oversized memory copy. It copies the untrusted io_size into corrected_size and unconditionally reads the first byte of hid_buffer, then when the report ID is zero as indicated by "hid_buffer[0] == 0" it performs "corrected_size--" without verifying that any data was received. Because the only size capping against hid_expected_size occurs before this decrement, a zero or too small io_size causes corrected_size to wrap to a very large value which is then used as the length for memcpy into hid_dest derived from transfer_priv. An attacker who can supply zero length or crafted HID data can trigger an out of bounds read and a massive copy that corrupts memory, resulting in process crashes or potentially arbitrary code execution.

The vulnerability is an empty constructor for the Chapters::Edition type in the WebM mkvparser that leaves object members uninitialized within Android mediaserver. The root cause is missing initialization of internal fields that are expected to hold safe default values and maintain class invariants. An attacker can trigger the flaw with a crafted WebM or Matroska file that forces the parser to read or act on these uninitialized members such as sizes, counts, or pointers. The internal control flow enters the constructor body and exits immediately with no assignments, so later parsing logic consumes indeterminate data which can lead to out of bounds access or invalid memory operations. This enables remote memory corruption that can cause a denial of service or facilitate arbitrary code execution as described by the Android advisory.

The code implements an improper global rate limit for TCP challenge ACKs, enabling a cross-connection side channel that weakens TCP session integrity. The root cause is the use of static shared state challenge_timestamp and challenge_count combined with a coarse per second window derived from the variable now computed from jiffies divided by HZ, so a single counter is reset and checked system wide rather than per socket. An attacker can trigger the issue by repeatedly sending spoofed in window segments to elicit challenge ACKs and observing when ACKs stop due to the shared limit, using that signal to infer valid sequence space. Because now gates both the reset of the counter and the decision to send an ACK, the resulting information leak facilitates blind in window probing and can lead to remote TCP session hijacking.

The vulnerability is a null pointer dereference caused by obtaining a transform pointer with const TransformPaintPropertyNode* clip_space = current_clip_->LocalTransformSpace and then using it without validation. The root cause is the unchecked assumption that LocalTransformSpace always returns a valid node, followed by immediate dereferences via EnsureCompositorTransformNode and taking the address of clip_space->NearestScrollTranslationNode. An attacker can craft rendering states that produce a clip with no local transform space so clip_space becomes null at runtime. Through the data flow from the initial clip and effect setup into the retrieval and use of clip_space, the code dereferences a null pointer, leading to a renderer crash and denial of service consistent with the Chrome CVE.

The code implements a lazily initialized singleton for the effect paint property root via the macro DEFINE_STATIC_REF, which is vulnerable to a data race and partial construction. The root cause is that this macro performs unsynchronized lazy initialization so concurrent calls to EffectPaintPropertyNode::Root can attempt initialization at the same time, resulting in double initialization or exposure of a half constructed object. The data and control flow show that the macro drives construction through Create and depends on nested calls to TransformPaintPropertyNode::Root and ClipPaintPropertyNode::Root, allowing interleaving across these paths during initialization. An attacker can trigger this by inducing concurrent rendering activity through crafted content, leading to crashes and denial of service in line with the Chrome advisory that unspecified issues could cause denial of service and possibly other impact.

The vulnerability is an absence of limits on the number of mounts in a mount namespace in Linux kernel fs/namespace.c before version 4.9, enabling unbounded creation of mount structures. It occurs because the recursive attach and propagation path in attach_recursive_mnt invokes propagate_mnt and commit_tree without enforcing any per namespace quota or cap on mount creation. An unprivileged user can trigger it by repeatedly issuing MS_BIND mounts on a shared mount, causing each operation to be propagated and reattached across peers and subtrees, leading to exponential growth in the number of mounts. In the shown logic when IS_MNT_SHARED is true the code propagates and commits mounts and then iterates over propagated children to commit them again without any count checks, allowing a simple bind mount loop to allocate unbounded kernel objects and tie up mount management. The impact is denial of service through excessive memory consumption and possible deadlock in the mount subsystem.

The function mkvparser::ReadUInt relies on the debug statement assert(pReader) to validate its reader pointer, which is compiled out in production, leaving the subsequent call to pReader->Read vulnerable to a null or invalid pointer dereference. The root cause is the absence of a runtime check for pReader, so an invalid pointer supplied via the function input can reach the virtual call site unchecked. A crafted MKV file processed by mediaserver can drive parsing into a state where this function is invoked with an invalid IMkvReader, and the data and control flow from the input parameter to pReader->Read then leads to a crash or memory corruption. In the Android libwebm context, this flaw can be exploited remotely to cause denial of service and potentially achieve arbitrary code execution.

The Linux kernel function parse_rock_ridge_inode_internal in fs/isofs/rock.c has a logic flaw in the handling of Rock Ridge relocated directory entries CL that can lead to an infinite reparse loop. When a CL entry is processed the code redirects parsing to the referenced inode and jumps back to the "repeat" label without any check for self reference or cycle detection. An attacker can craft an ISO 9660 image with a self referential CL entry so that each pass reencounters the same CL and restarts parsing indefinitely. This flawed control flow hangs the mount operation and creates an unkillable mount process which enables a denial of service.

The vulnerability is an incorrect thread safety enforcement in AcceleratedStaticBitmapImage::CheckThread used by Canvas that allows cross thread use of SkImage. The root cause is an unsynchronized flag detach_thread_at_next_check_ that controls a detach and implicit rebinding of the thread checker via DetachFromThread, which is then followed by a permissive check through CalledOnValidThread, effectively bypassing the intended thread affinity. An attacker can trigger this by driving a sequence of canvas operations from different threads so that when CheckThread runs with the flag set, it detaches, clears the flag, and the subsequent check succeeds on the wrong thread. The data and control flow of function entry to the conditional detach and flag clear enables thread unsafe access to SkImage, leading to data races and heap corruption that a crafted HTML page can potentially exploit.

The function aio_read_events_ring is vulnerable to an array index error that enables kernel memory disclosure to a local user. The root cause is that the untrusted ring header fields are read from a user mappable page and the value of head is used without validation to compute both indexing and copy sizes, for example pos is set to head + AIO_EVENTS_OFFSET and page is selected via ctx->ring_pages[pos / AIO_EVENTS_PER_PAGE] before any normalization by nr_events. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a very large head value through the mapped AIO ring and invoking an AIO read operation. The internal flow then indexes the ring_pages array out of bounds or computes an erroneous avail and copies data from the wrong kernel page with copy_to_user, leaking sensitive kernel memory.

The code contains a null pointer dereference vulnerability because it uses its Element pointer parameter without validation. At entry, the parameter e flows directly into the return expression that chains multiple tag checks including e->hasTagName and similar helpers, so if e is null the member access dereferences a null pointer. An attacker can trigger this by supplying crafted content that causes the upstream parser to pass a null or otherwise invalid Element pointer into this routine during document structure processing. The missing precondition check lets control and data flow from the function entry to the dereference proceed unchecked, resulting in a crash and denial of service with potential for other undefined impacts.

The Juniper GGSN parser in tcpdump contains a buffer over read vulnerability that stems from treating a variable length cookie as a fixed struct without validating its size. After juniper_parse_header fills l2info, the code casts l2info.cookie to a juniper_ggsn_header and immediately reads fields such as proto and the VLAN identifier, yet it never checks that the cookie holds enough bytes for that structure. An attacker can supply a crafted packet with a truncated or malformed Juniper header that still passes the initial parse, causing the subsequent protocol printing and switch on proto to access memory past the end of the cookie, with ndo eflag triggering additional out of bounds reads via EXTRACT_16BITS on the VLAN field. This can lead to tcpdump crashes or unintended disclosure of adjacent memory, resulting in denial of service or information exposure during packet analysis.

No vulnerability is evident in the provided code. The observer strictly guards against null dereference and mismatched notifications using the condition "if !popup_ || Details<ExtensionHost>(popup_->host()) != details return" which short circuits before accessing the popup host. It only processes the expected type EXTENSION_HOST_VIEW_SHOULD_CLOSE and invokes HidePopup under the validated condition while unexpected notifications are confined to a debug assertion path. Consequently there is no unsafe memory access path or attacker controlled data flow that could lead to exploitation or impact.

The vulnerability is an information disclosure in libstagefright where the BufferMeta constructor assigns the caller supplied flag is_backup directly to the internal field mIsBackup, causing the object to trust external input for buffer handling decisions. The root cause is a trust boundary violation and lack of validation or consistency checks of this control flag against the memory handle and port context, which can lead the media stack to skip copying, sanitization, or other safe handling of buffers. A local malicious app can trigger the flaw by providing a crafted is_backup value through media APIs so that a nonbackup or untrusted buffer is treated as a backup buffer, altering ownership and lifetime paths. Because the assignment flows unguarded from the constructor parameter into internal state and influences downstream logic that exposes or shares IMemory, an attacker may obtain access to residual or otherwise unauthorized data outside of its permission levels, consistent with Android ID A-29422020.

The function contains an information disclosure bug caused by unconditionally modifying the user visible message header length field with the statement 鈥渕sg->msg_namelen = 0鈥?without ensuring that any corresponding address or name data has been initialized. This write occurs immediately upon entry to the recvmsg handler and is performed directly on the msghdr supplied by the caller, with no validation or coordination with the preparation of ancillary address data. When the generic recvmsg machinery later uses the reported length to decide what to copy back to user space, this desynchronization between the length field and the actual initialized data can expose uninitialized kernel memory. A local attacker can trigger the flaw via recvfrom or recvmsg on the affected socket type to obtain sensitive kernel information.

The function contains a cross profile credential injection issue where the OAuth2 token service is obtained via GetForProfile using member profile_ instead of the passed in profile pointer. The root cause is a context mix up that uses handler state rather than the function parameter to choose the target profile for credential updates. When the sign in reason is reauthentication, unlock, or add secondary account the code proceeds to call UpdateCredentials with the received refresh token and writes it to the service selected with profile_ so the token can be stored under the wrong profile. An attacker who can induce this flow on a machine with multiple profiles can cause refresh tokens to be written to another profile leading to session hijack, cross profile account linkage, and potential privilege escalation.

The vulnerability is a buffer overflow in libpng functions that handle the PLTE chunk, specifically png_set_PLTE and png_get_PLTE, when processing a palette larger than what the IHDR bit depth permits. The root cause is insufficient bounds checking where the code uses the number of palette entries from the PLTE chunk without capping it to the maximum allowed by the bit depth, so memory is allocated or assumed for a small palette while copy operations use a larger count. An attacker can trigger the flaw by crafting a PNG with a very small bit depth in the IHDR header and an oversized PLTE chunk that declares more entries than allowed. The control flow first parses IHDR to set bit_depth and later processes PLTE using num_palette without reconciling the two, which drives out of bounds writes or reads during palette transfer and can cause a crash or potentially enable further memory corruption.

The vulnerability is an unsafe propagation of untrusted container metadata in Android mediaserver where a parsed MKV cue timecode is returned to callers without validation. The root cause is that CuePoint::GetTimeCode simply executes return m_timecode which exposes attacker controlled values directly to downstream logic that assumes valid ranges and invariants. A crafted media file can supply extreme or malformed timecodes that, once returned, are used in timestamp arithmetic, seeking, indexing, or allocation sizing during libwebm and libvpx processing. Because the function body returns the field with no checks, the data and control flow provide no mitigation, enabling integer wraparounds and out of bounds operations that lead to memory corruption with potential remote code execution or denial of service.

The function OnRegisterAgentError contains a logic flaw where it immediately decrements the connection counter using "--num_connecting_calls_" and uses that value to drive state transitions. The root cause is performing the decrement before validating that a corresponding in flight operation exists, with only a debug time DCHECK enforcing non negativity, which allows the counter to drop below zero in release builds. An attacker can trigger this by causing repeated or duplicate error callbacks for agent registration via external error conditions, leading to multiple invocations of this handler. The control flow then uses the decremented value to decide on notifying changes and proceeds to UnregisterAgent and run the error callback, so repeated calls can induce inconsistent state, spurious unregistration, and missed or incorrect notifications. The result is a denial of service against Bluetooth pairing and connection management, such as preventing new connections or tearing down active ones.

The function contains a memory leak in kadmind where the GSS name buffers are mismanaged, enabling denial of service through unbounded memory consumption. The root cause is that 鈥済ss_buffer_desc client_name, service_name鈥?are declared without initialization and the corresponding gss_release_buffer calls are not placed on the common exit path, so when setup_gss_names fails the function jumps to exit without releasing any allocations. An authenticated client can trigger this by sending a request with a NULL principal name, which drives the error path and leaves the client and service name buffers unreleased. Because the control flow bypasses cleanup after errors, repeated requests accumulate leaked memory and can exhaust server resources.

The vulnerability is an information leak caused by the media element logging routine that prints a raw object pointer and an unsanitized message to the media log. It occurs because the code logs the this pointer cast to void star and the message directly via BLINK_MEDIA_LOG without any sanitization or redaction. An attacker can trigger this by crafting a page that forces a media load failure or unsupported source, causing NoneSupported to run and forward cross origin derived details through the message. The function takes the message parameter as input and logs it unmodified before any state changes, leaking memory addresses and cross origin information, which can expose sensitive data and weaken address space layout randomization.

The issue is a buffer over read in tcpdump prior to 4.9.2 within ip_printroute when parsing IP route options. The root cause is inconsistent error handling and missing bounds enforcement, since only the check for length less than 3 returns, while later validations for bad length and bad ptr only log and allow execution to continue. An attacker can craft an option with length at least 3 but misaligned or with a malformed pointer so that the loop calls ipaddr_string on cp plus len while verifying only len less than length instead of ensuring that four bytes remain. Because control flows past the lone early return, the function reads beyond the end of the supplied buffer, leading to a crash or potential disclosure of adjacent memory and enabling denial of service.

The vulnerability is improper exception handling on the early error path, where the function returns via 鈥渞eturn V8Proxy::throwNotEnoughArgumentsError鈥?when too few arguments are supplied. The root cause is that this legacy helper is not bound to the current V8 isolate or context while other paths use isolate aware error setting, which can misassociate or drop the exception. It is triggered by invoking the method with fewer than two arguments, causing control flow to take the early return based solely on args length before any isolate aware handling is performed. As a result, an attacker can induce mis scoped exception propagation that may allow execution to proceed in an undefined state or crash the renderer, leading to denial of service and potential logic bypass.

Nautilus before 3.23.90 contains a file type spoofing vulnerability that allows a .desktop launcher to masquerade as a benign document, leading to unintended command execution. The root cause is that the UI displays the value of the Name field as the apparent filename while suppressing any indication of the .desktop extension, and the launch path does not enforce a user trust confirmation via the metadata::trusted flag. An attacker can provide a .desktop file with execute permission whose Name ends in .pdf and whose Exec field runs a malicious sh -c command, tricking the user into opening what appears to be a PDF. When clicked, Nautilus follows the launcher execution flow and runs the Exec command without surfacing the true file type or prompting the user for trust. This enables arbitrary command execution under the victim鈥檚 account and can lead to full user compromise.

The function restore_page_device is vulnerable because it performs critical operand and execution stack preflight checks only under the guard if "LockSafetyParams && !samepagedevice", which skips these checks when the page device remains the same. This flawed condition couples resource validation to a security flag and to whether a device change occurs, rather than validating unconditionally when subsequent operations may consume significant stack space. An attacker can craft PostScript or PDF content that keeps the device unchanged to bypass the checks and then drive interpreter actions that require many stack pushes. Since dev_old is derived from pgs_old and its LockSafetyParams together with the computed samepagedevice control the conditional, the code proceeds without ensuring available stack space, enabling stack exhaustion that results in bypass of intended access restrictions and potential denial of service.

The vulnerability is improper object lifetime handling in BlockEntry, where the destructor is defined as empty, for example "BlockEntry::~BlockEntry() { }", so no cleanup or state reset occurs when objects are destroyed. The root cause is missing teardown and possibly non virtual destruction semantics, which leaves owned buffers, indexes, or references unmanaged and creates lifetime mismatches between container structures and their elements. It is triggered when mediaserver parses a crafted WebM or Matroska file and destroys BlockEntry instances, control enters the destructor but no deallocation or invalidation runs, leaving stale pointers or inconsistent reference counts that subsequent parsing logic continues to use. This leads to memory corruption inside mediaserver, enabling denial of service and potentially remote code execution as described in the cited Android CVE.

The vulnerability is an incorrect cross layer call in the SPNEGO mechanism where the wrapper forwards its inputs directly to the generic GSS entry gss_get_mic_iov_length while passing the SPNEGO context handle unchanged. This occurs because the code relies on an inappropriate context handle, causing the mechglue dispatcher to recurse back into the SPNEGO path or to misinterpret the context and read through invalid pointers. It can be triggered by a crafted SPNEGO packet that leads the system to call this routine with a SPNEGO context, with all parameters propagated unchanged and no validation. The resulting control and data flow produce incorrect pointer reads or unbounded recursion, allowing a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via process crash or stack exhaustion.

The code contains a stack based buffer overflow in extractPages due to writing unbounded data into the fixed size stack buffer declared as "char pathName[1024]". The root cause is the use of sprintf to compose the output path into pathName using a destination template that incorporates attacker controlled data derived from the source filename, allowing the formatted output to exceed the buffer size. An attacker can trigger the flaw by supplying a crafted source filename that causes the generated destination path to be longer than the 1024 byte buffer during the page extraction loop. Data and control flow show that input from srcFileName influences the sprintf write into pathName, leading to memory corruption that can cause a crash and potentially allow remote code execution.

The function vrend_create_shader is vulnerable to an integer overflow that leads to out of bounds access. The root cause is unchecked arithmetic on attacker controlled fields offlen and pkt_length used in expressions such as ((offlen + 3) / 4), sel->buf_len = ((offlen + 3) / 4) * 4, and copy or bounds checks using pkt_length * 4 and pkt_length * 4 + sel->buf_offset, which can wrap and produce incorrect buffer sizes and comparisons. A guest can trigger the flaw by crafting offlen and pkt_length so the long shader decision and subsequent allocation size are computed too small while memcpy uses a larger length, or so the continuation size check is bypassed. This data and control flow causes writes or reads beyond the allocated buffer during shader assembly and results in a crash of the rendering process, enabling denial of service.

This code contains an information disclosure in rtnl_fill_link_ifmap caused by copying an only partially initialized stack structure to userspace. The root cause is the declaration and field wise initialization of struct rtnl_link_ifmap as in 鈥渟truct rtnl_link_ifmap map = { 鈥?}鈥?which leaves alignment padding bytes uninitialized. When the function later serializes the structure using a copy of sizeof map into a Netlink attribute, those untouched padding bytes are transmitted. A local user who can read the resulting Netlink message can obtain residual kernel stack data, exposing sensitive information.

The vulnerability allows the Linux kernel booted with UEFI Secure Boot to load untrusted ACPI tables appended to the initrd, enabling a bypass of Secure Boot restrictions and execution of unauthorized code. The root cause is the lack of signature verification or lockdown enforcement for ACPI table overrides that are sourced from the initrd when Secure Boot is active. An attacker can trigger it by appending crafted ACPI tables to the initrd image, which the kernel reserves and exposes early via the path that includes the call to "early_reserve_initrd", after which ACPI initialization accepts and installs these tables. The data flow maps the initrd early, the ACPI subsystem scans it for override tables, and the kernel loads them into the ACPI namespace, causing AML to run with kernel privileges. The impact is a violation of the secure boot trust model leading to execution of untrusted code and potential privilege escalation.

The code implements a security check that is supposed to verify whether media comes from a single origin, but it returns true when the media data source is absent, effectively failing open. Specifically, HasSingleSecurityOrigin uses the logic "if (data_source_) return data_source_->HasSingleOrigin(); return true;" which treats the no data source case as single origin. In the HLS path the player may not use data_source_, so a crafted page that loads an HLS manifest with cross origin segments triggers the default true result and bypasses the missing origin verification. This control flow causes Blink to treat cross origin HLS content as same origin, enabling a remote attacker to bypass the same origin policy and gain unauthorized access to media as if it were same origin.

MemoryInstrumentation::GetVmRegionsForHeapProfiler exposes a privileged operation without enforcing access control, allowing untrusted code to retrieve memory metadata. The root cause is the absence of authorization checks at the API boundary, as the function simply acquires a coordinator and forwards the request via "coordinator->GetVmRegionsForHeapProfiler(callback)" with no validation. A compromised renderer or other unprivileged caller can trigger it by invoking this entry point, which directly passes the provided callback and executes the sensitive query. As a result, an attacker can obtain VM region information from privileged processes, enabling information disclosure and potentially undermining ASLR and other defenses.

The code is vulnerable due to the interaction between a large 64 bit dividend computed as "u64 nsec = (u64)jiffies * TICK_NSEC" and a flawed x86 implementation of the helper div_long_long_rem in include asm x86 div64 h present in Linux kernels before 2.6.26. The root cause is an incorrect division routine that can raise a divide error fault when given certain 64 bit values, leading to a kernel panic. A local user can trigger it by invoking clock_gettime which calls this conversion routine, causing the unchecked product to flow into div_long_long_rem with NSEC_PER_SEC as the divisor. The data flow from the function parameter jiffies into nsec and then into the division exposes the bug and allows a non privileged caller to cause a denial of service.

The code contains an out of bounds read in ReadPropertyMSBLong that allows four bytes to be read from the input buffer without ensuring the underlying pointer remains within valid memory. The root cause is reliance on the bookkeeping parameter length to bound access while the loop performs "*(*p)++" four times after only checking "*length < 4," with no guarantee that length correctly tracks the actual remaining bytes for the buffer referenced by q. An attacker can supply crafted input that desynchronizes length from the real buffer end so the check passes and the loop reads beyond the buffer. Because line 1鈥檚 length parameter controls both the early guard and the subsequent decrements, this faulty data and control flow leads to an out of bounds read that can disclose adjacent memory, matching the described information leak.

The vulnerability is an incorrect object lifecycle management issue in Blink鈥檚 ImageBitmap loading path that can lead to use after free and heap corruption. The root cause is incomplete Oilpan garbage collection tracing in the Trace method, where only some fields such as "visitor->Trace(factory_)", "visitor->Trace(resolver_)" and "visitor->Trace(options_)" are marked, leaving another required GC managed reference or base class state unmarked and eligible for premature collection. An attacker can trigger this by serving crafted HTML that exercises ImageBitmap creation and asynchronous resolution, causing the loader to later access an object that the collector has already reclaimed. The flawed data and control flow arises when the GC omits a still in use object due to the incomplete trace and later code in bitmap loading or promise resolution dereferences the freed memory, allowing a remote page to induce heap corruption and potentially achieve code execution within the renderer process.

The vulnerability is a remotely triggerable denial of service in the rendering pipeline where GraphicsContext::fillRoundedRect unconditionally calls the stub "notImplemented()" during normal painting. The root cause is a missing implementation with no safe fallback, leaving a reachable crash point guarded only by the early exit "if paintingDisabled() return;". An attacker can craft page content such as CSS with floating styles to drive layout and painting into this rounded rectangle path, ensuring painting is enabled and the stub is invoked. The control flow from the paintingDisabled check directly to notImplemented allows external styling inputs to reach a crash site, enabling denial of service and aligning with the CVE context where floating style driven rendering can cause a crash or other unspecified impact.

This vulnerability is a use after free in Google Chrome PDF handling when processing interactive form fields. It occurs because objects representing PDF form fields or their annotations can be freed while references remain in event handling or rendering code, reflecting flawed lifetime management and missing ownership checks. An attacker can trigger the condition with a crafted PDF that drives a sequence of field updates and events so the object is destroyed and then accessed again during subsequent layout, painting, or scripting callbacks. The data and control flow routes an event that releases the object while another path later dereferences the stale pointer, causing memory corruption or a crash. Exploitation leads to denial of service and may enable arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the browser process.

The function request_key_and_link is vulnerable because it assigns the comparator field as ".match_data.cmp = type->match" without validating that type->match is non null. This unchecked function pointer is later invoked during the lookup path via search_process_keyrings and keyring_search_iterator, so a key type with a null match field will cause a null function pointer dereference. A local user can trigger this by causing a key request for a type that lacks a valid match callback while providing a description that leads the code down the direct lookup path. The data flow from the untrusted type parameter into the comparator and its subsequent use in the search logic results in a kernel crash, enabling denial of service and as described for this issue potentially facilitating privilege escalation.

The vulnerability is a kernel denial of service in hash_accept where the code unconditionally exports a hash state via crypto_ahash_export even when no data has been processed. The root cause is the lack of state validation or initialization checks before performing the export during accept, so a request tied to the parent socket can remain uninitialized if the socket has received zero bytes. A local user can trigger this by creating an AF_ALG hash socket, selecting an in kernel hash algorithm, and calling accept without sending any data. Through this control flow the function derives the request from the socket context and immediately exports and then imports it for the new socket, leading the crypto backend to access invalid state and causing a kernel oops that results in denial of service.

The provided function does not contain a vulnerability. It simply forwards the JNIEnv pointer to another routine via the call "return RegisterNativesImpl(env)" without performing any stateful operations, memory manipulation, or input dependent logic that could be abused. There is no data or control flow within this snippet that could trigger an error condition because the only data passed is the JVM supplied env pointer and the return value is propagated unchanged. Any exploitable behavior, such as unsafe native registration or misuse of a null or invalid JNIEnv, would reside within RegisterNativesImpl or its callers, not in this wrapper, so no attacker impact can be achieved through this code alone.

The function SplitUrlAndTitle is vulnerable to a null pointer dereference due to relying on the debug-only assertion "DCHECK(url && title)" to validate its output pointers. In release builds this check is absent, so if a caller passes a null url pointer the subsequent call to url->assign dereferences a null pointer. The data flow from the url parameter directly into the assign operations is unguarded, and the control path does not add any runtime validation beyond the removed assertion. An attacker who can influence the call site to supply a null url can cause a crash, resulting in a denial of service.

The function that constructs a path string is vulnerable to an integer overflow that leads to a heap based buffer overflow in Git before 2.7.4. It appends user influenced path and name into a strbuf via strbuf_addbuf and strbuf_addstr without validating that the computed target size fits in the integer type, which can result in an undersized allocation followed by an overlong write. An attacker can supply an extremely long filename or induce many nested trees so that the combined length wraps during size arithmetic and the subsequent append overruns the heap buffer. Because the function body always performs the final append of name after optionally adding path, the cumulative length from both inputs flows unguarded into the growth and copy operations, enabling memory corruption and potential remote code execution.

The vulnerability is a Subresource Integrity bypass in Chrome where PendingScript::notifyFinished consults memory cache metadata that records only that an integrity check occurred rather than that it succeeded. The root cause is a flawed trust decision that treats the occurrence of a prior integrity check as equivalent to a successful verification, allowing cached resources to be marked trusted without validating their cryptographic hash.
