An attacker can trigger this by causing the same resource to be loaded twice so that the first load populates cache state and the second load reuses that state to skip or short circuit integrity verification. This control flow lets a tampered script be accepted from cache and executed in the context of the page, enabling script injection and arbitrary code execution despite declared integrity requirements.

Chrome鈥檚 IDN spoof checker in the URL Formatter mishandles visually confusable characters, enabling domain spoofing via IDN homographs. The root cause is an incomplete and weakly validated transliteration rule set used to normalize confusables, built with UnicodeString::fromUTF8 from a non ASCII rule string such as "[镁霞覐] > p; [魔薪褯遥谣訄訆詪鸳冤] > h;", where creation errors are only guarded by a debug time check so release builds can proceed with missing or invalid mappings. Data and control flow in the constructor reuse a shared status and continue after the rule construction step, which leaves certain Cyrillic or Greek lookalikes unmapped and thus not normalized during spoof checks. An attacker can register a crafted internationalized domain name that uses these omitted characters to appear indistinguishable from a trusted domain and have it displayed as legitimate.

The vulnerability is a logic error in Blink where frame access is granted after a Same Origin Policy check without also verifying that the target frame is hosted in the same renderer process. The root cause is that the checks in BindingSecurity and DOMWindow validate origin and then expose or cache direct frame or window references while assuming same process invariants that are not enforced. An attacker can craft a page that forces two same origin frames to be placed in different renderer processes and then trigger code paths that bind to or access the foreign frame. This missing process check allows cross process object references to pass through DOM bindings and later be dereferenced as if they were intra process pointers, leading to memory corruption and renderer crashes that result in denial of service and potentially enable further exploitation.

The code contains an integer overflow that leads to heap memory corruption when packing RPC messages. The root cause is the 32 bit computation of the total packet size, as in 鈥渦int32_t pkg_size = RPC_PKG_HEAD_SIZE + pkg->ext_size + pkg->body_size,鈥?where ext_size and body_size are influenced by untrusted input and can cause the sum to wrap around, producing a too small pkg_size. This incorrect size drives the allocation of send_buf, yet subsequent memcpy operations copy ext_size and body_size bytes based on the original large values, overflowing the allocated buffer and corrupting heap memory. An attacker can trigger this by supplying crafted size fields in an RPC package, resulting in denial of service or potentially arbitrary code execution.

The function contains a check then use race that can lead to a null dereference or use after free when determining TTS state. It trusts the result of the guard condition "if (chromeos::CrosLibrary::Get()->EnsureLoaded())" but then reobtains the singleton and calls "GetSpeechSynthesisLibrary()->IsSpeaking()" without retaining or validating the same instance, leaving a window where the library pointer can be null or invalid. An attacker can trigger this by causing concurrent initialization or teardown of the CrosLibrary or by inducing rapid state changes so that the library becomes unavailable between the check and the use. Because the boolean guard controls entry to the dereference but does not enforce object lifetime or perform a null check, the code can crash, yielding a denial of service similar in effect to previously reported Chrome issues that result in process termination.

The code in pin_remove corrupts fs_pin list consistency by deleting a hash list entry without validating or restoring the node state, which violates internal list invariants in the fs_pin implementation. The root cause is the use of hlist_del on m_list while holding pin_lock with no check that the node is still linked and no reinitialization, leaving stale pointers that permit double deletion. The control flow acquires the lock and immediately deletes from the list with no guard, so a later invocation or alternate cleanup path that attempts to unlink the same node acts on an already unlinked element and damages the list structure. A local user with user namespace root can trigger this via umount2 with the MNT_DETACH flag during filesystem pin cleanup, leading to list corruption that causes a kernel crash and denial of service.

The bytecode interpreter contains an out of bounds memory access in its virtual machine memory handling. It reads an index from untrusted bytecode into r1.i and then uses it directly to access mem[r1.i] in opcodes such as OP_CLEAR_M, OP_ADD_M, OP_INCR_M, OP_PUSH_M, OP_POP_M, and OP_SWAPUNDEF without validating that the index falls within the allocated MEM_SIZE. An attacker can craft a rule whose bytecode supplies an index outside the valid range or truncates operands so the interpreter also reads an eight byte immediate past the end of the code buffer while advancing the instruction pointer with no bounds checks. Because ip is initialized from rules code and each opcode path immediately consumes and applies the unvalidated operand, the data flow directly leads to memory corruption or a crash, enabling denial of service and potentially arbitrary code execution.

This vulnerability is an improper list cleanup in the ALSA timer stop path that leaves stale list entries after a stop or close, which can crash the kernel. It occurs because _snd_timer_stop checks the slave flag and then clears the RUNNING flag and executes goto __end, leaving the instance in ack_list and active_list instead of unlinking it. A local user can trigger this via a crafted ioctl that stops or closes a timer instance, especially a slave one, which leaves dangling list links. As the function skips the unlink operations yet still performs notification after releasing locks, later traversals of these lists access invalid instances and the system can crash, resulting in a local denial of service.

An uncontrolled format string vulnerability exists in the Condor function display_sigset because the logging call passes the parameter msg directly as the format string to dprintf. The root cause is misuse of the variadic logging API, where a fixed format such as "%s" is not used and untrusted data is supplied as the format. An attacker who can influence msg can include format specifiers that, after only a null check, are forwarded to the logging sink. This direct data flow from the function parameter to dprintf allows interpretation of attacker controlled directives, leading to denial of service, information disclosure, or potentially arbitrary code execution.

Vulnerable description: The vulnerability is a defect in Chrome鈥檚 download pipeline where downloaded files are saved without the Mark of the Web, allowing bypass of OS level protections that rely on zone metadata. It occurs because the code path that writes downloads to disk fails to set the Windows Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, meaning the security zone information from the network context is not propagated to the file writer. An attacker can host a crafted HTML page that triggers a download through a renderer initiated or otherwise misclassified path that is then persisted without the required zone tag. This data and control flow omission results in files being treated as trusted local content by the operating system, suppressing warnings such as SmartScreen or Protected View and enabling an attacker to increase the likelihood of arbitrary code execution or policy bypass when the user opens the file.

The function leaks GSS name buffers on error paths because the cleanup of client_name and service_name is placed before the common exit label. Specifically, the code calls setup_gss_names and on failure or on a NULL principal that causes krb5_unparse_name to fail it jumps to the label exit_func, which bypasses the calls to gss_release_buffer and leaves the buffers allocated. This control flow means that requests which trigger early returns such as those specifying a NULL principal cause the routine to skip freeing resources allocated for client and service names. An authenticated attacker can repeatedly send such requests to accumulate leaked memory in the kadmind process and cause a denial of service through memory exhaustion.

The function krb5_gss_wrap_size_limit contains a null and lifetime validation flaw, as it dereferences a caller supplied context pointer without checks in the statement "if (!ctx->established)". The root cause is that context_handle is cast to ctx and its fields are accessed immediately with no verification that the handle is non null or still valid. An attacker can trigger this by supplying malformed or stale GSSAPI context traffic so that an invalid or freed handle is used here, a scenario made more likely by the handle lifecycle issues described in the CVE for krb5_gss_process_context_token. Because untrusted input flows directly into a pointer dereference, this can cause a denial of service through a crash and, when combined with use after free conditions from the broader handle mismanagement, can potentially lead to more severe memory corruption and code execution.

The vulnerability is an improper RIP update in the KVM x86 emulator where em_loop calls jmp_rel with ctxt->src.val directly, allowing an unvalidated relative displacement to dictate the jump target. The root cause is the lack of enforcement that the LOOP family uses a signed 8 bit immediate which must be correctly sign extended and validated before use. A guest can trigger this by issuing a crafted LOOP or LOOPcc so that after RCX is decremented and the condition evaluates true, the code executes the jump using the attacker controlled ctxt->src.val. The control flow only vets RCX and flags while the displacement flows unmodified from ctxt->src into the jump, enabling unintended RIP changes and out of bounds instruction fetch. The result is a guest denial of service through an emulator induced crash.

The vulnerability is a NULL pointer dereference in the Aiptek driver probe routine that allows a physically proximate attacker to crash the system by connecting a crafted USB device with no endpoints. It occurs because the code assigns endpoint = &intf->altsetting[0].endpoint[0].desc and immediately uses fields such as bEndpointAddress and bInterval to build an interrupt URB without verifying that the interface reports any endpoints or that the first endpoint is a valid interrupt IN endpoint. This logic lets untrusted device descriptors drive control flow directly into dereferencing an invalid endpoint entry, causing a kernel fault when the endpoint array is missing or shorter than expected. The impact is a reliable denial of service through a system crash upon device insertion.

The vulnerability is an integer overflow in the pointer adjustment inside gray_render_span that can lead to out of bounds memory writes. It occurs because the code computes p using signed arithmetic and then adds rows minus one times pitch without validating ranges or detecting overflow. An attacker can trigger this via a crafted font that supplies large or adversarial bitmap dimensions and a nonnegative pitch, causing the multiplication to wrap and place p outside the bitmap buffer. Data and control flow amplify the error as y helps form the initial p, the conditional for nonnegative pitch applies the faulty adjustment, and the rendering loop driven by count and spans writes bytes using FT_MEM_SET or unrolled stores to the miscomputed address, resulting in a crash or possible code execution.

The Linux kernel i8042 driver contains a race condition in i8042_start that improperly publishes device state and enables time of check to time of use errors. The code sets "port->exists = true" and then executes a memory barrier, but placing the barrier after the store and without paired acquire operations on readers fails to provide proper release semantics, so other CPUs may observe the flag change while related state remains invisible or can change after validation. Because the pointer to the shared structure is taken from serio port_data and subsequently used by readers that first check the exists flag, concurrent execution can lead to inconsistent or uninitialized accesses and a NULL pointer dereference resulting in a system crash. An attacker can exploit this by racing device interactions that validate the exists flag and then use the port fields, achieving denial of service and possibly other unspecified impact.

The function AXNodeObject::textFromDescendants contains a logic flaw where children are skipped only if aria-hidden equals the literal value "true" via the comparison equalIgnoringCase, which fails to normalize or parse the attribute according to ARIA boolean rules. As a result, providing aria-hidden values that are semantically true but not exactly "true" after case folding such as values with leading or trailing whitespace allows the code path to bypass the continue and proceed to accumulate the child鈥檚 text. The control flow first reaches the child iteration, evaluates the flawed check, and then appends text using either recursiveTextAlternative or textFromDescendants, thereby incorporating content that should have been excluded. An attacker who controls DOM attributes can exploit this to expose text intended to be hidden from assistive technologies, leading to information disclosure and inconsistent accessibility behavior.

The function encrypted_update dereferences a payload pointer from a key that may be negatively instantiated, which violates the KEYS subsystem expectations for update paths. It assigns epayload from "key->payload.data[0]" and then reads fields such as "epayload->master_desc" and copies "epayload->payload_data" without verifying that the key is positively instantiated or that the payload pointer is valid. A local attacker can craft keyctl operations to negatively instantiate an encrypted key and then trigger this code path, causing the unvalidated pointer to be dereferenced during comparisons and memcpy calls and leading to a kernel BUG or crash. This enables denial of service and in some configurations can be abused to escalate privileges.

The function contains a heap buffer overflow due to a mismatch between the allocated buffer size and the amount of data written during rendering. It allocates q using image->rows and a stride derived from image->columns, but invokes ddjvu_page_render with a rectangle defined by external w and h, so if rect.w exceeds image->columns or rect.h exceeds image->rows the renderer writes past the end of q while the code ignores the return status. The root cause is the lack of validation and synchronization between rect dimensions and the buffer layout, compounded by unchecked casting of w and h to unsigned and unguarded use of the computed stride. An attacker can craft a file that supplies oversized or inconsistent dimensions to force ddjvu_page_render to overflow q, after which the code copies the corrupted data into the image and finally calls "if !image->ping SyncImage image", committing the corruption and leading to a crash and denial of service.

The code is vulnerable due to an incorrect teardown order in sctp_net_exit where the control socket is destroyed after its dependent SCTP per net resources have been freed, specifically calling sctp_free_addr_wq and sctp_free_local_addr_list before invoking "inet_ctl_sock_destroy(net->sctp.ctl_sock)". The root cause is that the ctl_sock destructor path relies on per net state such as address workqueues and local address lists that are no longer valid. A local user can trigger this by creating SCTP sockets and then causing a network namespace teardown or similar SCTP shutdown, which leads the ctl_sock destruction to run after the dependent structures were released. This data and control flow results in a use after free in the socket destruction path, causing kernel panic or memory corruption and enabling denial of service.

The code in MPEG4Extractor::readMetaData contains an unchecked memory allocation that can lead to a null pointer dereference and denial of service. The root cause is allocating with malloc using a size derived from file controlled data and then immediately writing to the returned pointer without verifying success. An attacker can craft an MP4 with many or very large PSSH entries so that psshsize becomes large enough for malloc to fail, after which the code executes memcpy into a null buffer. The data flow is from parsed mPssh entries to psshsize, then to char *buf = malloc(psshsize), followed by memcpy into buf without a null check, enabling a remote crash of mediaserver and potentially a device hang or reboot.

The relocs function contains a heap based buffer overflow caused by allocating the GOT table for n_got 32 bit words but then using it as an array of struct reloc_struct_t and writing multiple fields per element. This under allocation arises at the allocation of got_table and is followed by writes to addr_to_patch and data_offset for each i in the loop, which overrun the allocated buffer when n_got is at least one. An attacker can craft a binary that sets the GOTPIC flag and controls object fields so that get_ngot_entries returns a chosen n_got, the sanity checks are passed, the undersized allocation is made, and the loop stores per entry data into the mis sized array. This can lead to heap corruption, application crash, and potentially further impact such as arbitrary code execution.

The function sem_getref is vulnerable because it acquires a raw spin lock on sma->sem_perm.lock with spin_lock and later releases with ipc_unlock while performing an IPC RCU refcount update, creating a mismatched locking context. This breaks the locking semantics required by the IPC RCU refcount helpers and, together with the flawed refcount handling in ipc_rcu_putref in kernels before 3.10, enables races and refcount imbalance. A local user can trigger the issue by crafting semaphore activity that drives concurrent sem_getref and refcount put paths so that the refcount is changed under the wrong lock semantics. The control flow takes the lock unconditionally, modifies the refcount, then unlocks via a different API family, which can cause premature frees or leaks leading to memory consumption or system crash.

The code contains a null byte pathname handling flaw that allows an attacker to bypass filename validation and open unintended files. The root cause is a mismatch between length aware parameter parsing using the format string "sllll" and subsequent use of the raw C string in php_stream_open_wrapper, with no rejection of embedded NUL characters. An attacker can supply a filename containing %00 followed by an allowed extension so that any checks on the full string pass while the open operation truncates at the NUL and resolves a different path via stream_resolve_include_path. This data flow from user input to file opening without NUL sanitization matches the filename NUL extension class of issues and can lead to arbitrary local file disclosure under the privileges of the PHP process.

The function jas_matrix_asr is vulnerable because it relies on assert-based preconditions rather than runtime checks, leaving critical constraints unenforced in release builds. If a caller supplies a negative or excessively large n or a matrix whose dimensions are positive while rows_ is null, the loops compute rowstart and data from unchecked rowstep and then execute "*data = jas_seqent_asr(*data, n)" which can perform an invalid shift or dereference invalid memory. The control and data flow trust numrows_, numcols_, and rowstep to guide pointer arithmetic without validation, so malformed or attacker influenced matrix state propagates directly to out of bounds accesses. An attacker who controls the inputs that populate the matrix or the shift count can reliably cause a crash and may be able to corrupt memory.

The get_build_id function in Android Debuggerd contains a stack based buffer overflow when parsing the GNU build ID note from an ELF file. The root cause is the use of a fixed size 128 byte stack buffer, for example "uint8_t build_id_data[128]", while using the untrusted Desc Size field n_descsz as the copy and iteration length without bounding it to the buffer size, and only validating the unrelated Name Size field. An attacker can craft an application that supplies an ELF PT_NOTE entry of type NT_GNU_BUILD_ID with a Desc Size larger than 128, causing the code to copy and process more data than the buffer can hold and overflow the stack. Because the logic reads the note header, enters the NT_GNU_BUILD_ID branch, and operates directly on n_descsz with no protective check, the resulting memory corruption in the debugger process can be exploited to crash the system or gain elevated privileges.

This code is vulnerable to an out of bounds read in OpenSSL through 1.0.2h when parsing ServerHello extensions in ssl_scan_serverhello_tlsext due to incorrect pointer arithmetic based boundary checks. The root cause is that the generic guard allows data plus size to reach exactly the buffer end, while the ec point formats branch immediately dereferences one byte from the payload via *sdata++ without first enforcing a minimum length and only later checks that the parsed length matches size minus one. An attacker can craft a ServerHello that includes a TLSEXT_TYPE_ec_point_formats extension with size set to zero and positioned at the end of the extensions so that the check data + size > d + n passes and the first read occurs past the buffer boundary. This data and control flow permits a remote crash leading to denial of service and the broader misuse of pointer arithmetic and length handling in related paths can also lead to integer overflow and other unpredictable effects consistent with the cited CVE.

The code contains an object lifetime flaw that can lead to a use after free in the DevTools handler path, matching the Chrome DevTools network handler issue. The root cause is reliance on a raw pointer process_ that is only checked with "if (!process_)" and can remain non null after the underlying object has been destroyed. An attacker can craft a page that exercises DevTools and triggers this handler while racing process or frame teardown, causing the null check to pass and the code to dereference process_ to obtain the storage partition and background sync context and then post work to another thread, thereby operating on freed memory. This control flow enables memory corruption and can be exploited for arbitrary code execution.

The vc4_get_bcl function contains an integer overflow that leads to a heap buffer overflow when processing user supplied command list sizes from the VC4_SUBMIT_CL ioctl. The root cause is that shader_rec_offset is computed by rounding up bin_offset plus args->bin_cl_size using 32 bit arithmetic before any effective bounds validation, while the subsequent guard starting with if uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset || only checks later derived offsets and never verifies that the initial addition did not wrap. An attacker can trigger this by supplying a very large bin_cl_size so the addition overflows, producing a small shader_rec_offset and consequently a too small allocation, after which copy_from_user copies bin_cl_size bytes into the bin buffer and overruns the heap. Because the validation relies on already wrapped values derived from user controlled input, a local user can cause kernel memory corruption leading to denial of service or possibly more severe impact.

The vulnerability lies in EnableSecureTextInput, which unconditionally enables secure keyboard entry by invoking frame->Selection().SetUseSecureKeyboardEntryWhenActive(true) after only a null frame check. The root cause is missing precondition and lifecycle enforcement, as the code does not verify that the element or frame is focused or active and provides no corresponding disable, allowing the secure input mode to persist beyond its intended scope. An attacker can trigger this by invoking the function in background or hidden contexts or across rapid element lifecycles to leave secure input mode stuck on. Because the control flow only gates on a non null frame, this privileged state change can lead to user interface disruption and denial of service consistent with the reported Chrome pre 46 issues.

The function contains a memory leak that can be triggered by a request with a NULL principal name, leading to denial of service through memory consumption. After setup_gss_names allocates the GSS buffers client_name and service_name declared as gss_buffer_desc, a failure in krb5_unparse_name when arg->rec.principal is NULL causes a jump via goto exit_func. Because the gss_release_buffer calls are placed before the exit label, this error path skips the releases and leaks the allocated buffers. An attacker who sends repeated authenticated requests with a NULL principal can therefore cause cumulative leaks, exhausting server memory over time.

The vulnerability is an information disclosure in the BPF verifier where do_check logs instruction details via print_bpf_insn without enforcing the allow_ptr_leaks policy. It occurs because do_check does not propagate or check allow_ptr_leaks to restrict output, so when the code executes the path guarded by log_level and calls print_bpf_insn insn it may print sensitive kernel addresses. A local user can trigger this by submitting crafted BPF programs through the bpf system call with verifier logging enabled, causing the verifier to iterate instructions and emit their details. This control flow from the log_level gate to print_bpf_insn yields unredacted pointers in the verifier output, enabling attackers to infer kernel address layout and undermine KASLR, facilitating further kernel exploitation.

The vulnerability is a synchronization flaw in Chrome on Windows prior to 20.0.1132.43 that allows sandboxed processes to interfere with one another during GPU channel establishment. The root cause is the constructor initializing the coordination primitive as auto reset and initially non signaled with "event(false, false)" which is unsuitable when multiple waiters must be released once a shared resource becomes ready. It is triggered when multiple sandboxed or renderer processes concurrently wait on this event because a single signal awakens only one waiter and early signals are not latched, causing the remaining waiters to stall indefinitely. Since this configuration is hard coded at construction and governs the entire object lifecycle, the control flow systematically propagates the race prone behavior across all instances. An attacker can exploit the contention by inducing repeated channel establishment to cause denial of service and cross process interference.

The code is vulnerable because it manipulates huge page state in the PMD without first validating or safely synchronizing that state, which can lead to a bad PMD during fault handling under KVM and crash the host. Specifically, it calls "split_huge_page_pmd" on the computed PMD for address 0xA0000 and only afterward evaluates "pmd_none_or_clear_bad", then immediately proceeds to map and modify PTEs, so the control flow can act on an inconsistent PMD that may be concurrently faulted. A guest with administrative control can trigger repeated page faults on huge page mappings that exercise this path, causing "pmd_none_or_clear_bad" interactions and leaving the kernel to handle corrupted PMD transitions. The impact is a host denial of service as the kernel hits a bad PMD during the fault path and crashes.

The prep_reprocess_req function in the MIT Kerberos KDC contains a denial of service flaw in its service principal realm referral logic. The root cause is an API mismatch where a C string copy routine is applied to krb5_data components that are length delimited and not guaranteed to be NUL terminated, copying the first principal component into a heap buffer sized to the component length plus one. A remote authenticated attacker can craft a TGS REQ whose server principal has two components and passes the canonicalization checks, causing the code to allocate a buffer for the first component and invoke strlcpy on it. Because strlcpy expects a NUL terminated source yet the input is only length delimited or may be NULL, the copy scans past the buffer or dereferences a NULL pointer, leading to an out of bounds read and a KDC crash that enables denial of service.

The function cpStripToTile in LibTIFF tiffcp contains an integer overflow that leads to a heap based buffer overflow. The root cause is the use of narrow 32 bit counters and signed skews defined as "uint32 rows, uint32 cols, int outskew, int inskew" combined with unchecked pointer arithmetic, which allows size and stride calculations to wrap and leaves copy loops operating on inconsistent buffer sizes. A crafted image can supply oversized dimensions or skew values that overflow upstream allocation or stride computation, after which the routine copies rows times cols bytes using "*out++ = *in++" and advances pointers with "out += outskew" and "in += inskew" beyond the allocated heap region. Because the parameters from the signature directly drive the loop counts and pointer adjustments with no bounds or overflow checks, the data and control flow culminates in out of bounds reads or writes, enabling a crash, memory corruption, or possible remote code execution.

The code contains an iterator invalidation vulnerability caused by modifying the container while iterating over it. Inside the loop over axes_data_ the call to TryAddAxesButton in the condition if "TryAddAxesButton(button_id, AxesRequirement::kRequired)" may insert or erase entries in the same container that provided button_id, which invalidates the active range based iterator. The flaw is triggered when an unused button id is encountered after the "IsUsed(button_id)" check and TryAddAxesButton performs a mutation, leading to undefined behavior on the current or subsequent iterations. This control flow can result in crashes or memory corruption, enabling a denial of service and potentially opening a path to more severe exploitation depending on allocator behavior and attacker influence over the input that drives button addition.

The code exhibits a data race in the extensions guest view where CancelPendingTask unconditionally dereferences shared state and can corrupt the heap. The root cause is the lack of synchronization and state validation before calling "filter_->ResumeAttachOrDestroy" with element_instance_id_ and MSG_ROUTING_NONE, assuming filter_ remains valid across concurrent tasks. A remote attacker can craft HTML that drives overlapping attach, cancel, and destroy events in the guest view so that CancelPendingTask races with teardown and accesses a freed or inconsistent filter_. Because control flows directly from function entry to this call without any checks, the race leads to use after free and memory corruption, resulting in browser crashes or potentially arbitrary code execution.

The vulnerability is an out of bounds pointer computation in libvpx where a method returns a raw pointer into the input buffer using unchecked arithmetic, effectively input_ plus BorderTop times kOuterBlockSize plus BorderLeft. The root cause is the lack of bounds and overflow checks on values influenced by untrusted media input, allowing BorderTop and BorderLeft or their product to exceed the allocated frame buffer. A crafted media file can set frame and border parameters so the returned pointer is invalid and later read or written by image processing routines, because no validating control path constrains these offsets before use. This leads to memory corruption in the mediaserver process and can be exploited for denial of service or remote code execution.

The function is vulnerable to a use after free caused by constructing a persistent file system entry from a transient object with unsafe lifetime semantics. At the call to "GDataEntry::FromDocumentEntry" a raw pointer obtained from a scoped pointer is passed into the factory, and if the factory retains references instead of performing deep copies, the underlying DocumentEntry is destroyed when the function returns while the newly created GDataEntry is stored in the directory and later accessed. This is triggered by invoking AddUploadedFileOnUIThread with an entry that gets converted and then added to the parent directory where subsequent operations read identifiers and hashes, causing the new entry to reference freed memory. The graph relations show that the vulnerable construction is driven directly by the function inputs with no lifetime validation which allows the dangling reference to propagate into later directory and cache operations. An attacker able to supply or influence the DocumentEntry can cause a denial of service via a crash or potentially achieve code execution through controlled reuse of freed memory.

The code is vulnerable to a NULL pointer dereference in the handling of the xkb_geometry section, allowing a crafted keymap to crash the xkbcommon parser. The root cause is that CompileKeymap assumes the XkbFile objects for each section have valid non NULL fields and unconditionally uses them, for example logging with "Compiling %s \"%s\"" which dereferences files[type]->name and then invoking compile_file_fns[type] without validating internal pointers. An attacker can supply a keymap where the geometry section is parsed into an XkbFile whose critical members are NULL, so after the presence check passes, the subsequent logging or compilation step dereferences NULL. The control flow collects section pointers, verifies only that each required section exists, and immediately uses their contents, which leads to the flaw when the geometry section is malformed. The impact is a reliable denial of service by crashing any consumer of the vulnerable library.

This code contains an unchecked return value flaw in the call to "asn1_push_tag" when encoding an ASN.1 BOOLEAN. The root cause is that the function does not verify whether the tag push and its underlying memory allocation succeeded and continues unconditionally to "asn1_write_uint8" and "asn1_pop_tag". The data and control flow show that the result of "asn1_push_tag" directly feeds subsequent operations with no guarding condition, so a failed push leaves the encoder in an invalid state that is then written to, leading to state corruption or invalid memory access. In the Samba AD DC LDAP server a remote attacker can craft packets to induce allocation failures in the ASN.1 layer, triggering this path and causing excessive memory consumption and a crash that results in denial of service.

The function retains an SkImage and records the executing thread but dereferences an unvalidated thread pointer at the statement "thread->ThreadId()", making the code vulnerable to thread misuse and null pointer dereference. The root cause is missing validation of Platform::Current()->CurrentThread() combined with reliance on unrelated DCHECKs that do not ensure the thread is valid, which allows recording an invalid or absent thread context. This can be triggered when the function is invoked on a path where no platform thread is registered or during startup and teardown, causing a crash, or by causing the image and its context to be used across threads unsafely. Because execution flows from retrieving the SkImage to using the thread pointer without a guard, a crafted HTML page that drives Canvas code into this state can lead to crashes or heap corruption consistent with the described thread unsafe SkImage handling.

The code in fs/pipe.c is vulnerable to denial of service because it lacks aggregate limits on memory consumed by pipe buffers across the system. In pipe_fcntl the F_SETPIPE_SZ command takes the user supplied arg, rounds it to a pipe size, derives nr_pages, and calls pipe_set_size to expand pipe->buffers after only enforcing capability and a per pipe maximum. Since there is no per user or global accounting of unread pipe data, an unprivileged user can create many pipes and repeatedly request larger non default sizes, then leave the buffers allocated and filled. This data flow from arg to pipe_set_size enables unbounded cumulative memory growth across pipes, allowing a local attacker to exhaust kernel memory and cause system wide resource starvation or crashes.

The vulnerability is a race condition in the UDP send path where per socket IP option state is read and used without proper synchronization while network traffic is being processed. In udp_sendmsg the code harvests per message options and otherwise uses inet->opt to drive routing and skb construction, but most of this path executes without the socket lock, allowing concurrent setsockopt calls on the same socket to modify or free those option structures. A remote attacker can trigger this by sending traffic to an application that changes socket options during activity, causing the send path to dereference stale option data during route selection and packet construction. This unlocked data and control flow from message control data into ipc and then into routing and buffer creation enables use after free and memory corruption, resulting in denial of service through slab corruption and a kernel crash.
